subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I regret to announce the closure of the commercial fishery dependent on salmon runs returning to a number of the famous producing rivers in the maritime provinces. This course of action has been forced upon us by a serious decline in the number of salmon returning to the Saint John, Miramichi and Restigouche Rivers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext:
Because much of the salmon fishery in the Port aux Basques area of Newfoundland is also dependent on these runs destined for mainland streams, it, too, will be closed beginning in May of this year.
While the situation will be reviewed annually, it is expected that at least one full cycle, namely six years, will elapse before the stocks in these rivers will be rebuilt to the point where large-scale commercial operations can commence once more.
The advice of existing river management committees on which the fishermen themselves serve will be sought not only in respect of the duration of these closures but also as to the manner in which the runs can best be rehabilitated.
Compensation will be paid to commercial fishermen whose earnings are affected by these river closures. Payments will be negotiated on an individual basis and the formula which will be employed will be worked out in close consultation with the fishermen themselves.
These closures will not apply to salmon returning to the streams in Newfoundland and Labrador. They do not apply, also, to salmon returning to the rivers in Nova Scotia.
Historically, the total mainland take accounted for approximately one-half of the over-all catch of Atlantic salmon by Canadians. This volume has been sharply
reduced. It has fallen by more than 80 per cent since 1967. On the Miramichi, where escapements formerly were measured in the tens of thousands of large fish, they are now measured in the hundreds.
There are several reasons why our stock of large mainland salmon has become seriously depleted. They are: first, heavy fishing by foreign nations on the high seas; second, heavy fishing by our own commercial fishermen; and third, pollution in some of our own main salmon rivers themselves.
We are moving quickly to deal with pollution. There has been a significant improvement in water quality on the Miramichi, for example. But commercial fishing, especially on the high seas, is another story. In spite of agreements to the contrary, the catch by Denmark alone was four times that of all of our own mainland fishermen last year.
The estimated cost of this program for the current fiscal year, 1972-1973, is in the order of $2 million. Over 900 commercial fishermen are involved. This announcement is being made now in order to avoid unnecessary expenditures by our fishermen in preparing for the Atlantic salmon fishery in 1972.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: It comes too late. They have already spent their money.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: I have already made arrangements, Mr. Speaker, to meet with fishermen from the affected areas in Chatham, New Brunswick, on Thursday of this week.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I feel certain that all members of the House who have an interest in preserving the stocks of Atlantic salmon listened with interest to the statement just made by the Minister of Fisheries, which outlines in detail the present government's method of dealing with this problem. We also deplore the fact that this statement has only now been made in the House. The announcement has already appeared in the press and was made known on Friday night's television news. This shows complete disregard for this House, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext:
Quite frankly, all of us who represent ridings in Atlantic Canada are keenly aware of the need for carrying out salmon conservation policies. However, we in the opposition are deeply concerned about the hamhanded, halfhearted, slipshod restrictions imposed from year to year by this government not only on our salmon fishermen but also on Canadian fishermen in general. We have seen the removal of the sick mariners' benefits, the salt subsidy and the fishing bounty, and restrictions have been

April 24, 1972
Atlantic Salmon Fishery Closure
placed on our haddock fishery, our seal fishery, our swordfishing industry and, now, on our salmon fishery.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext:
The minister has said that this drastic action is forced upon us by the serious decline in the salmon fishery and especially by the heavy fishing by foreign nations on the high seas. This raises the question, Mr. Speaker: When did information concerning Danish fishing for salmon on the high seas first become available? According to an article which appeared in the Saint John Times-Globe of June 10, 1965, Mr. Larry Guptill, then the vice-president of the Nova Scotia Salmon Anglers Association, told a meeting in Halifax that the discovery of the Atlantic salmon feeding grounds by Danish seiner fishermen off the coast of Greenland in 1964 would before long do irreparable harm to the Atlantic salmon fishery. This warning was repeated over and over again by representatives of our party from Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Quebec, but no action was taken. Even in 1969, Mr. Speaker, when the delegate from Denmark with brutal frankness told the conference of nations that fish for the North Atlantic salmon, "When the salmon are gone, we'll fish for something else", our two Rip Van Winkles, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the Minister of Fisheries, did nothing.
Denmark has no salmon rivers and the Danes are overkilling salmon which originate in Canada, the United States, the United Kingdom and other countries. This problem, therefore, is an international problem. But owing to blind greed on the part of the Danes, inadequate international law, and a disinterested, lackadaisical Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Atlantic salmon, the king of fish, is threatened with extinction.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: There are too many sardines in the government.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext:
Has the Secretary of State for External Affairs or the Minister of Fisheries taken the time to point out to the Danes that without Canadian, American, British, Irish or Scottish rivers and without the enormous cost that is being paid to protect and improve these rivers, there would be no salmon? Salmon that originate from other countries simply would not be sufficient to maintain world stocks.
The minister has told us that the principal country now, and for some time past taking Atlantic salmon on the high seas is Denmark. However, there are also considerable catches by Norway and by Sweden. Both Denmark and Norway are members of the 15-nation commission known as ICNAF, or the International Commission for the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries. Under ICNAF and NEAFC, the North East Atlantic Fisheries Convention, the North Atlantic fishing nations are pledged to co-operate in protecting and conserving the fish stocks of the North Atlantic. With the facts fully documenting the actual decline of the Atlantic salmon population and with Canada urging a total ban on fishing for salmon on the high seas, are we to take it that ICNAF and NEAFC are no longer operating, or that these countries sign these agreements only as windowdressing while continuing to pillage, plunder and

rape our fisheries resources until nothing is left? In fact, the Danes are calling the tune but we are paying the piper.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext:
Once again this government is engaged in one of its familiar tactics-confrontation with the Canadian fishermen. Being law-abiding citizens they will do as the law dictates, but there is little satisfaction in purchasing salmon fishing gear and in getting a ship ready for the salmon fishing season only to learn that the government has unilaterally decided to close down the salmon fishery and buy up the fisherman's equipment. This action only replaces his capital outlay. It leaves him asking the question, "Where can I go, what can I do now, how will I provide for my own and my family's needs?"
Before this drastic action was taken by the government I believe that a commission should have been established in Atlantic Canada to look into the fisheries problems of that area, with special attention being given to the problems of our salmon fishermen. I also believe that the salmon fishermen concerned should have had an opportunity to be heard and make their wants known, not as the minister stated on Thursday after this fait accompli, but before this action was taken.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: I thank you for your comment, Mr. Speaker. I have almost concluded my remarks. This government was elected on the promise that it would practice participatory democracy. I think it is high time it started practicing what it preached.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was rather surprising to find the minister rising in his place today to make a statement on motions on a decision which we all understood was a fait accompli. However, I presume he decided the matter was of sufficient importance to formally announce it in the House, even though belatedly. As one who has some interest in and concern for the welfare of the fisheries of Canada, it crosses my mind immediately that this announcement may be a foretaste of similar action on the Pacific coast of Canada. I hope that is not so.
The minister has announced action that can only be described as drastic. It may be necessary. One cannot argue that. It seems to me there are two basic positions that can be taken in light of the continued exploitation of this fishery by the Danes. I expressed one of them in a conversation with an ardent conservationist in the United States when I visited there last fall. He suggested that we have no fishery for Atlantic salmon. I noted that as an American he was part of the people who destroyed their own salmon fishery and perhaps they should not take it too much amiss if Canadians decided what we should do
April 24, 1972

with ours. In light of the situation that exists I told him that one of the courses Canada could follow would be to take our share while the salmon lasted. This, of course, would be a very difficult decision for us to make. However, I am inclined to say to the minister and the government that unless our action shames the Danes into taking reciprocal action, the only course left to us may be to alter this decision and take what there is left of the salmon while we can get them.
I am somewhat puzzled, in view of the decline in the spawning runs to streams such as the Miramichi disclosed in the minister's statement, that the minister should have made no reference to what is to happen to the sports fishery in those streams. It seems to me his statement is similar to others I have heard the minister make in connection with salmon fishing on the Pacific coast. The only restrictions he seems interested in imposing there are on commercial salmon fishermen. He seems to be of the view that sports fishermen should be allowed to run wild. I should have thought it appropriate for the minister to have referred to what will happen to those salmon which will hopefully still escape to spawn after they are in the streams themselves. To me this is as important as what will happen to them on the high seas.
I know I cannot attribute blame for this situation to this minister.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: Go ahead!

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: I would remind the House, though, that some of us have been trying to warn those concerned for a long time that this sort of thing would happen unless effective action were taken. When the original North Atlantic Fisheries Commission was established some of us pointed out that its terms of reference were basically inadequate. From my point of view, ever since action was taken to ratify that treaty Canadian governments have been most remiss in pursuing the development of that commission to the point where it would be able to exercise effective control over the catch on the high seas. Listening to the vigorous statement made today by the spokesman for the official opposition, I wished he could have taken the same vigorous approach in 1964 when some of us were trying to prod the government into taking effective action which might have helped to forestall the situation described in the minister's statement.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext: We did.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CLOSURES IN ATLANTIC SALMON FISHERY
speechtext:
There is not much more I need to add. I hope that consequent upon the measures taken by the Minister of Fisheries vigorous action will be taken by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and by the government as a whole to place before the forums of the world the actual facts of what is happening to the marine resources of the oceans and to indicate that Canadians simply cannot tolerate this kind of improvidence and that we are prepared to use any and every means at our disposal to ensure not only in our own interest but in the long-term interests of the human race that the despoliation of the resources of the sea does not continue.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should just like to say a few words on this subject. The minister's statement greatly surprised me and I suppose he had serious reasons for making such a major announcement today. I believe the fishermen affected by the decision are far from happy, even with a promise of compensation. Nevertheless, according to the minister's statement, more than 900 commercial fishermen will be involved, which means that roughly 1,500 to 200 wage earners will need retraining because six years is quite a long period and I believe the families affected by the decision will be in a rather critical situation.
I hope the reasons leading the minister to take such a serious, rigorous decisions are important. I am not sure the minister has given us the exact reasons for his decision, or at least I did not understand them. In fact, there were reports in last week's papers which greatly surprised me. Apparently there are reasons external to the situation and foreign elements have tampered with the spawning sites of salmon.
I therefore urge the minister once more to take whatever steps are necessary and to use his present experience in this region in order to prevent the same thing from happening elsewhere.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, it is a statement. I must say it is a very short one indeed, just explaining the

April 24, 1972
Social Security Agreement With Germany
agreement in very general terms; it is a couple of paragraphs long. In view of the shortness of the statement and the fact that there is nothing controversial about it I did not distribute copies of the statement.
In accordance with the terms of the Convention, on March 30 in Bonn our ambassador exchanged our instrument of ratification with the German authorities. As a result, the agreement enters into force on May 1, 1972. Under this agreement many Canadian citizens of German origin will for the first time be able to enjoy benefits they earned under German social security schemes before they came to Canada.
The German pension programs to which the convention applies are the wage earners', salaried employees', miners', and the steelworkers' supplementary insurance. The Canadian programs to which the convention has application include the Canada Pension Plan, the old age security plan and the Quebec pension plan. Generally speaking, these plans now provide for the payment of benefits abroad.
The primary responsibility for the administration of the convention has been given to the Canada pension plan branch of my department. In Quebec, the corresponding responsibility for administration has been given to the Quebec pension plan. Advertisements and other public announcements will appear shortly.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT WITH FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for the statement though I regret I did not see a copy of it before it was made. My only comment is that while we welcome the agreement with the federal Republic of Germany it would certainly be helpful for many people resident in Canada if we could have a similar deal with the United Kingdom.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: TABLING OF AGREEMENT WITH FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY-STATEMENT BY MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one who has been pressing for this agreement for a considerable period of time I should like to say that we welcome the fact it has been entered into and that the minister has now been able to table copies of the agreement in the House.
As the minister pointed out, the purpose of this reciprocal agreement is to make it possible for pensions that were earned in Germany to be received by Canadians of German origin who have now become Canadian citizens, and for the opposite to happen if Canadians who earn pensions here move to that country. A great many former Germans who have become Canadian citizens will benefit from the provisions of this treaty, and on their behalf we welcome its coming into force.
I note that the effective date, as indicated by the minister, is May 1, 1972. Many of those who are affected by this arrangement will be sorry the date was not much farther back. Some of them have lost many years of pension rights. Of course, in negotiations there are two sides and I can only assume that the Canadians who did the negotiating got the best deal they could.
Like the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, I express the hope that this reciprocal agreement in the field of pensions, which has now been made between Canada and the

Federal Republic of Germany, will be the forerunner of reciprocal agreements with the United Kingdom, France, the United States, Italy and perhaps a number of other countries. I congratulate the minister for having established in his department a division which deals with international social security. This is a field that could become even more important as the years go on. We welcome this announcement today and on behalf of those who will benefit from it we express appreciation that this agreement has been concluded.

AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS-INCREASE IN WAGES AS RESULT OF STRIKE
speechtext:
1.	How much of an increase in wages (a) did the air traffic controllers want (b) were they offered?
2.	What was the settlement wage to the air traffic controllers?
3.	What was the difference in dollars between the amount offered and the amount accepted in the settlement?
4.	How much did the average air controller (a) lose as a result of the strike (b) gain as a result of the increase received over and above the amount offered before the strike began?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS-INCREASE IN WAGES AS RESULT OF STRIKE
speechtext:
1.
(a) The original wage demand of the air traffic controllers was for an increase of 46 per cent on July 1, 1971 and 14.5 per cent on July 1, 1972, for a new contract extending from September 30, 1971 to September 30, 1972. (b) Treasury Board offered the recommendation of the majority report of the Conciliation Board which was as follows: 5 per cent October 1, 1971, 5 per cent July 1, 1972, 5 per cent, April 1, 1973. The union rejected it.
2.	On January 22, 1972, both sides agreed to the following settlement: 6 per cent October 1, 1971, 5.5 per cent July 1, 1972, 5 per cent April 1, 1973, which the union said they would recommend to their membership. The membership rejected it. The issue was referred to binding arbitration and the arbitrator's award was the same as the January 22 settlement namely, 6 per cent October 1, 1971, 5.5 per cent July 1, 1972, 5 per cent April 1, 1973. There was, therefore, no difference in the percentage increase but the arbitrator added two additional steps to the salary scales.
3.	There was no difference in dollars between the amount offered and the amount accepted in the settlement other than the two additional steps which provide for individual, not general, increases on or after October 1, 1973, for employees at the maximum of their salary scale. In 1973 an estimated 1.2 per cent will be added to payroll costs by the implementation of the new increments.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
April 24, 1972

That because the Government has failed to produce measures to create employment, has failed to encourage investment in Canadian industry, and has caused widespread uncertainty as to its economic programs, this House lacks confidence in the ability of the Government to meet the needs and challenges of the seventies.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion gives us an opportunity to look at the performance of the government and, hopefully, to provoke some constructive response and constructive action from the government. It gives us a chance to examine how the performance of the government stands up in the light of its mandate which, of course, was a wide ranging mandate given to it by the people of Canada.
The government has spoken of the concept of the just society. Speaking in terms of the economy may I say that, surely, the mandate and responsibility given by the people of Canada to this government involved at least the provision of a reasonable degree of economic opportunity for the people of this country, associated, of course, with a reasonable degree of stability. Surely, Mr. Speaker, the government was given the responsibility to manage the economy, to develop it and to continue the development of the Canadian economy for the good of all Canadian^. That mandate, that responsibility, was a broad one. It certainly included the effective and informed management of our economy, together with concern for social justice in Canada which, of course, includes such matters as regional disparity which, by the agreement of all, continues unabated; and this failure is one of the most marked failures of this government.
Of course, the promise went much further. It offered visions of the just society and of a united Canada. The government hinted that it had some secret for getting the economy of the country moving in a way that no other government had ever succeeded in doing. There was to be a new dimension of greatness that the government knew how to tap, if only we could be patient and trusting. Several times since then, of course, the government has told us that we were on the verge of greatness in this country. Somehow, this greatness seems to have escaped us. In view of this falling down on responsibilities, and in view of continuing high unemployment, I think it is kinder to draw a veil over some of these visions. This government has tapped no new veins; it has certainly taken us in no new directions-at least, it has not taken us in any direction in which anyone in his senses would wish to go.
This afternoon I want to look at what the government has accomplished in terms of plain effectiveness, which is a smaller but still very important area, in terms of economic management and in terms of the minimum degree of foresight that one would expect from the government. I have touched upon some of the mandates and responsibilities that the government was given. However, there were other responsibilities, other mandates, other directions, that the government was not given. Certainly, it was not given the mandate to create and maintain, month after month, the most serious unemployment, that this country has seen over a decade.
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT

speechtext: Four years after this government took office following the election, we have seasonally adjusted unemployment at 6 per cent. We have 43 per cent of the massive number of unemployed under the age of 25, although they constitute about 23 per cent of the work force. That in itself would shock any government, except a government as complacent as this one.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Forty per cent of the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who are out of work have been so for more than three months. The government did not have a mandate to create and maintain these conditions. It did not have a mandate to use one part of its responsibility, that is to control inflation, as an excuse to slow down the whole process of economic growth in Canada for a substantial period of time with savage consequences for the people of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: This government did not have a mandate to confront, confuse and harass Canadians in sector after sector of our economy and section after section of our country, discouraging investment and slowing down the rate of investment until, from indications for the first quarter of this year, it now seems that the impulse behind the recovery that was taking place is slowing down while unemployment remains high. Already, the more optimistic forecasts that were made about the real growth of our economy in 1972 are being modified, principally as the result of the failure of investors in this country to respond. This government certainly did not have a mandate to do this. It has done it to the detriment of the Canadian economy and the misfortune of all the people of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: Of course, the crux of the matter is the existence of massive unemployment in this country where it ought not to exist.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I am glad my great benefactor and colleague, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay), is here. I was about to do a little reviewing as far back as the summer of 1970.
I found it necessary to call the attention of this government to the serious extent to which unemployment had climbed at that time as a result of the slowdown adopted in 1969. After the budget in the fall of 1970, we expressed keen disappointment over the fact that the government was so complacent and was doing so little to stimulate the economy.
At the beginning of 1971, I felt it necessary to warn the government that unless it took urgent steps to get the economy moving, and we gave some details as to what steps should be taken, including substantial tax reductions, seasonally adjusted unemployment in this country

would not fall below 6 per cent in the year 1971. That prediction was based simply upon the application of common sense to independent forecasts of growth in relation to forecasts of growth in the labour force made by the Economic Council of Canada. Those forecasts were greeted with ridicule by the then Minister of Finance and the government. The complacency exhibited by this government during 1971 was probably without parallel, at least in living memory.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: They said they were willing to put their jobs on the line that the situation would improve steadily, and that the seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment would fall steadily throughout 1971. They saw no need to change their policies. If we were told once, we were told five times that the corner was being turned or that the corner had been turned. As it turned out, it was not a corner at all. It was simply a vicious circle on which the government had been taking the country round and round.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The prediction which I felt necessary to make is, unfortunately, still true today. Unemployment, seasonally adjusted, is still 6 per cent. The government's refusal to do anything adequate last year to fight unemployment was inexcusable. However, in light of its record, I do not suppose it could be called unexpected. For years the Economic Council of Canada had been warning the people and the government of Canada about the growth that would take place in the work force in 1965 and through the years. These predictions turned out to be true. The growth that took place in the work force in 1970-71 was in line with what had been usually taking place each year in this country since 1965.
The decision of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government to slow down the economy, and thereby create massive unemployment, was especially tragic in Canada in view of the forecast increase in the work force. The increase in the work force makes it much more difficult to catch upon the unemployment once it has been created. This makes it doubly hard for me to understand the complacency with which this government created unemployment in the first place, and then set out to stubbornly resist doing anything about it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: The government must have known in advance what was going to happen, but it took no effective measures. Therefore, could we really expect this same government to take effective measures once unemployment had risen to the massive proportions that it did? I suppose, Mr. Speaker, that would be like expecting a turtle to fly.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
It was much more in character for this government to whine, complain and use the labour force figures for its own political ends and that is what it tried to do. What is it doing now? What has this government

been doing recently with regard to the unemployment that has persisted at such high levels? The Prime Minister keeps talking about the thousands and thousands of jobs that are available, if people would only take them. He talks vaguely in terms of a leisure society which is supposedly in the process of being created, almost as if he were admitting that massive unemployment in this country is something planned, something that is associated in some way with progressive development in this country. That is the way the Prime Minister feels. I leave that opinion to be shared only by himself. As for me, his government, it is obviously lost.
It is not only the Prime Minister who is making these aimless statements. It is the government as a whole. There is fairly good evidence of aimlessness in the increasing insistence by various ministers, including the Prime Minister, I think, that we now need year round programs of the sort suggested by LIP, seasonal programs which, at least in principle, have great merit on a seasonal basis. It is now being increasingly suggested that we are going to have these kinds of programs on a year round basis. This is certainly an admission of defeat by the government in its quest for policies to provide jobs.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: On the basis of the information that has been made public, I think it is clear in Canada today that the sector of the economy that is weakest is the sector of investment. According to the government's own surveys, investment is expected to amount to about the same in 1972 as it was in 1971. It is clear that if there were to be a substantial increase in investment there would be a substantial increase in jobs. To me, it is also clear that the failure of the government to increase investment commitments is a reflection of the lack of confidence by the people of this country in the government of this country; it is a consequence of uncertainties, some of which the government has created and others of which it has deliberately allowed to continue. For the government to say there is a need for year round programs of an improvised type such as LIP is, I contend, an admission of defeat. Not only is it an admission of defeat by the government, it is a herald of ever-larger government expenditures-not expenditures to encourage economic growth and restore a larger measure of confidence, but expenditures brought about merely to prevent the governmental system, or, at least, the system of this government, from collapsing around its head. And, of course, this kind of expenditure to support year round programs of the kind I have mentioned inevitably means higher taxes for the already hard-pressed Canadian taxpayer to bear.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Even when its ministers are talking about a year round LIP program, community programs and so on, the government cannot change its bureaucratic spots. Even in this area the big brother attitude remains predominant. If the government feels there are local programs which are desirable and which cannot be adequately financed on a local basis, the sensible thing would be to meet with the provinces and with the municipal govern-

ments with a view to enabling those governments to finance such programs rather than sitting around in Ottawa like a group of big brothers deciding what is good for various local communities. Even in putting forward what the government likes to think is an imaginative, humane program, its members cannot escape from their own tradition of centralization.
The main point remains. The government seems to have virtually given up its attempt, if it ever really made one, to achieve anything like full employment. This is bad enough, but I am afraid there is worse to come. Incredible as it may seem, the government does not even learn from its own mistakes. At least this is true in the case of the Prime Minister who, a few weeks ago, refused to rule out the possibility of following again the same economic policies as he applied back in 1969, if he thought they were warranted. There could be no better example of the crying need for a new governmental approach. There is a crying need for new government leadership. Not only has the Prime Minister and his administration failed to provide positive leadership in encouraging an upward movement of the economy and the creation of jobs, but they are dragging the country deeper and deeper into a morass of uncertainty and confusion.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: So far, the government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) have refused to tell members of this House or the Canadian public whether or not a budget will be presented this spring. It should be a full employment budget, if one is brought down at all. I want to be frank about it. I have seen enough budgets presented by this government to know better than to expect that anything of any great value will ever come from a budget presented by them. But the government unquestionably has a responsibility to parliament, and to the people, to present in this House an accounting of its financial expectations for the year in which we are now living, the year 1972-1973, as well as an explanation of its plans for this year, if indeed it has any plans.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext: It should be a full employment budget, if one is brought down at all. Then again, despite repeated promises, monotonous promises, we have yet to see the government policy on foreign investment, yet the Prime Minister keeps telling us it was decided last December. Third, we still do not know where we stand with regard to trade relations with the United States, though the President has made it very clear that substantial differences exist between the two countries.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: The Prime Minister does not even know who is being heckled.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The Prime Minister is talking again. I thought he might have been reading. We are apparently re-opening negotiations with the United States, or at least we are thinking about it. We are told studies are being made. But from then on, a wall of secrecy comes between us and the facts. At least, it looks like a wall of secrecy from the outside. But I suppose if one were really inside the government it would look more like a swamp than a wall. There have certainly been no indications otherwise, and in the meantime the Canadian economy faces continued uncertainty in this area. This is coupled with uncertainty about the budget and uncertainty about foreign investment.
Next, there is the famous, or rather the notorious, tax reform bill which was passed by the use of closure last year. It was one of the first times a major bill has been passed before it was even ready and we are still waiting for the regulations; we are still waiting for the amendments which the then minister of finance promised would be placed before parliament. Where are those amendments? Rumour has it that there are 100 amendments being considered by the government. The lawyers and the chartered accountants made a presentation which I think involved 300 amendments to that bill. Have these, too, been put away in some pre-electoral limbo where the government would like to keep them safely out of sight while it does its magic tricks during the campaign?
Then, there is the competition bill which is vanishing and re-appearing from time to time. Where does that bill stand now? What are the changes that are going to be made? I think the Canadian people as well as Canadian business have a right to know. Is the bill somehow or other being sawn in two by the government? Are we going to hear a scream one of these days from behind the curtains, so to speak, or is the plan to bring it back some day at the convenience of the government, uncut, to dazzle some and perhaps bedevil others? We can joke about these things, Mr. Speaker, but these are sources of great uncertainty in this country.
I do not want the Prime Minister to think that I am bringing these things up to dissuade him from calling an election, because I think-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: That would be the best thing that could ever happen to this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I accept what the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) says. I am bringing these things forward to show how little can be expected from this government in the future. It has drifted, it is drifting now, and it will continue to drift as long as it is able to cling to power. Instead of performing its duty of removing the uncertainties that exist, the government has been adding to them.
Of course, the Prime Minister has done something. He has moved some of his ministers around. He has given us a very personable Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner). But I must say that while I used to be pretty critical of the

April 24, 1972
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
former Minister of Finance, I sometimes regret that he is not still in that portfolio. Because, after all-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: He would give us some answers.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
No, he would not necessarily give us answers, but he sometimes did admit that he didn't have the slightest idea what was happening. That kind of refreshing candour has completely disappeared. I do not want to accuse the present Minister of Finance of being intentionally devious in his replies, but I have to say to him very bluntly that it is not good enough to go around giving general assurances about full employment and whatnot, while at the same time doing absolutely nothing about it. Any time he finds two or three businessmen gathered together, he joins them to tell them that they are really very fine fellows and to assure them that the government has their best interests at heart.
It is not the personality of this minister or of that one which is really basically at issue. What is basically at issue is the existence of a government whose only consistency is lack of effectiveness and whose only direction is the way in which a ship goes without a rudder. The rudder that is missing is not only personal; we need a commitment to action in the immediate future. We need a commitment to the restoration of confidence and the elimination of uncertainty. In the longer haul we need a real commitment to the development of a long-term strategy; one, for example, which will do something effective to fight regional disparity in this country. After some four years in office, some members of the present government are finally beginning to talk about industrial strategy. They find the phrase apparently popular in some quarters. But what we need is a real commitment, a commitment involving consultation with the various sectors of the economy and with the provinces. We have not had it; indeed, we have seen no sign of it from this government.
Such a strategy must involve several things. I have mentioned regional disparity. It must also include the whole pattern of our trade relations in the future. This involves looking outwards to see that there are prospects in terms of trading and trading blocs. We want something more than the "guff"-if you will excuse me for saying so, Mr. Speaker-that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) has been getting off when he speaks about institutionalizing our relations with the Common Market. When he is questioned about what this means, he says it means establishing the same kind of relations that we have with the United States. We do not need any more of that kind of confusion.
Such a strategy also involves looking inwards at ourselves, at our own potential for specialization and excellence with regard to goods and services. It involves our whole educational system as well, of course, as foreign investment policies. It includes other things too, things relating to our quality of life and the environment. We need a strategy for harmonizing the diversity of the people of this country. It has to include our plans for our north and middle north and the Canadians who want to inhabit those regions, not something that the Prime Minister throws out casually from time to time about some vision of the north. Such a strategy includes all these things, which is why I blame the government for its past

and present aimlessness and say that this country can no longer wait for the government to rise out of its lethargy.
Some people say that you cannot do anything about the unemployment which exists in this country, and I am afraid that is the attitude of this government. I sometimes feel the government regards the unemployment that exists as simply something relating to statistics. The government must be completely incapable of imagining the feelings of heads of families who are out of work and of young Canadians suffering frustration. All this has to come to an end. We have to create a climate of confidence in this country. We have to establish a relationship with meaningful consultation between the federal and provincial governments and between the government and various sectors of the economy and society. That condition alone cuts out any possibility of the present government ever achieving anything worth while in this area. It has alienated too many people. This government has sown too much distrust in this country at too many levels.
There are a good many kinds of non-confidence motions, Mr. Speaker, but the one I am presenting today- and I will be just a minute, Sir-is something special. It is not merely a parliamentary motion of non-confidence. The motion that I am presenting represents non-confidence in this government for its past policies and for its future prospects. It also represents non-confidence, lack of confidence, not only on the part of members of this House but also on the part of labour, agriculture, business, all the people of this country who gain their living or are trying to gain it. It represents a lack of confidence on the part of the provinces and regions of this country. It represents a lack of confidence in this government on the part of all the people in this country.
I started today by speaking of the mandate under which this government took power. This government has not only failed to fulfil that mandate; it has broken it by its mismanagement of the economy and by its total lack of sensitivity, its total lack of purpose throughout its life since 1968. The government has broken its mandate and has broken its faith with the Canadian people and, Sir, it is high time it went.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say something about the needs and challenges of the seventies to which the motion refers, and to try to measure the performance of the government, and indeed of the official opposition, in the light of those considerations. The issues raised in this motion underline the differences in social philosophy and approach between my party and both the government and the official opposition. Like the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), we have no confidence in the government's ability to meet the needs and challenges of the 1970's. But I want to make it clear that neither have we the slightest confidence that the Conservatives could possibly do any better.
Indeed, Sir, I remind you and the Leader of the Official Opposition that when you look for a comparable period of unemployment in the post-war period you find it in the years of the Conservative government between 1958 and
April 24, 1972

1962, so there is nothing in the record to show that the people who produced that mismanagement of the economy and that unemployment then are capable now of acting differently. I look around the leader of the opposition for the wizards of that party who would change the kind of thing it did during 1958 to 1962 and I cannot find them. Despite the charming smile of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees), there are no such beings.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: There isn't even a Wizard of Oz.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Precisely because the Leader of the Opposition emphasized that his motion, since it is moved at this time in this parliament, is not merely an expression of the lack of confidence in this government by members of this House but of the people of Canada, I want to say as clearly as I can that I am no more impressed by the promises of a phony incentive society than I was by the promises of a phony just society which I heard in 1968. We are all for justice and all for incentives, but I ask the same question: Justice for whom and incentives for whom?
It is clear that the Leader of the Opposition is preparing to appeal to the Canadian people for a chance to do exactly the same thing as the government has done, to start on a program of incentives for private corporations, and of that we have had enough. Every year the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, (Mr. Marchand) the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin), the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Benson), other ministers and heads of other departments hand out to the corporations of Canada, most of them foreign owned, literally hundreds of millions of dollars; I am certain if it were added up, more than 1,000 millions of dollars each year, with very little result in jobs or welfare.
Indeed, what we have in Canada today in my view is a corporate welfare program which has produced few jobs and even greater inequality in our society. What we have both from the government and the Conservative side is a promise of more of the same; more concessions to those corporations in the tax field and in other fields. My colleagues and I have no use for that kind of program, whether it comes from one side or the other. If I may, Mr. Speaker, let me put it to you this way. In my view, Canadians have watched the same play for over a century. We have learned that merely changing the cast of characters does not improve the play. Whether the lines are read with Liberal arrogance or Tory incompetence, it still remains a bad play for the life and the people of Canada.
I said during the debate on the Speech from the Throne that the Trudeau years have been wasted years, characterized by complacency, unconcern and cynical statements about the availability of jobs when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), should have known, if he did not, that for every available job, even if it was available for people out of work, there were 10 or 12 unemployed people looking for work. The reason I have on occasion been bitter and certainly sharp in my criticisms of the government and the Prime Minister, and I admit it, is that it seemed to me there was a complete lack of appreciation of what unemployment means in the lives of people. Tragedy of unemployment, especially for the young, is not
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
only the loss of income, which can be compensated partly by unemployment insurance benefits, welfare payments and the like, it is the loss of status as human beings which enforced idleness produces. I have in mind enforced idleness as distinct from the leisure time about which the Prime Minister talks and cynically equates with unemployment.
Enforced idleness means loss of self-reliance and loss of self-respect. It means loss of meaning and direction in the life of the person out of work. This is the tragedy that this government has deliberately created for hundreds of thousands of Canadians or, if our calculations are correct, for about 2 million Canadians in 1970 and 1971, because about 2 million Canadians were in fact out of employment for one period or another during each of these years. Today, we find that the secondary economic indicators, which originally promised to go up and hold out some hope for a real improvement in the economy, are down, showing that we have not even begun seriously to climb out of the difficulty into which this government deliberately placed us in its futile fight against something it called inflation without, in my view, realizing what the modern society is all about.
What are the needs and challenges of the 1970's? Because time will not permit me to deal with so large a subject fully, I want to suggest to you several obvious and very basic things our Canadian people have to turn to in the years ahead. These are not in any order of priority. First, we must face the fact that the children of the postwar baby boom have reached adulthood and put additional pressures on the labour market and on social needs such as housing, urban transportation and health care.
Second, we have technological developments in our society, increasing automation and cybernation in industry and all services, which affect not only the question of jobs for our people but also the life style of Canadians. They affect the equitable and appropriate division of work and perhaps the reduction of the work day, week or year and, therefore, the need for the creative development of programs for leisure caused by automation and cybernation in present and future years.
Third, we have increasing problems in our urban society; overcrowding, pollution, traffic jams, the lack of urban transportation, the lack of adequate parks and playgrounds for our children, the lack of day care centres for mothers who wish to go on the labour market and the lack of centres for our senior citizens in which they could not only live in decency but also in which they could fulfil themselves through some useful activity in our society. We have the entire complex of oppressive, modern factors endangering life in our increasingly difficult urban centres.
Fourth, we have also the threat to Canadian rural life and rural communities by the growth of corporate farming and by policies, both private by these corporations, and public by this government. These policies are deliberately aimed at reducing our already low farm population, making farming a kind of conveyor belt operation, instead of being concerned with the lives of farming people and the life style of farming communities, which are an integral part of Canada.

April 24, 1972
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
Fifth, we have the growing difficulties and dangers of pollution of our air and water caused, I emphasize, not only by industry and not only by vehicles that we may use, but caused also by our failure as a country, a failure mainly due to the inactivity of federal governments, to build the necessary recycling and treatment plants in the communities across this country. In the result, our rivers and lakes, like the Ottawa River next door, are polluted not only by industry but by the very life of the community because we dump our garbage and refuse into the waters which surround our cities and smaller towns.
Sixth, we have the immense problem of the increasing alienation of people in our society as a result of the bigness of our society: big government, big corporations, big unions, big universities, huge cities and the overwhelming and oppressive bigness which modern technological development has produced in our society. To this I add, the failure of governments oriented toward corporations instead of toward the people seriously to look for ways and means in which the people might break through the huge bureaucracy in every walk of life in our present society.
Seventh, we have a continuing problem in holding our country together, not only through new constitutional arrangements because constitutions are not things which hold people together. They are merely a framework which may or may not help. What we need in order to hold our country and people together is an effective attack on regional disparity, an effective attack on inequality across this country and a determined and committed attack on poverty throughout Canada. It is only when we have begun to solve these economic problems that any constitutional rearrangement can serve a useful purpose in holding our country and our people together.
Finally, in the 70's we face the urgent need to end the domination of Canada's economy by foreign corporations, mainly from the United States. This domination endangers not only our economic future, takes from us not only the capacity to shape our own priorities and our own investment direction, but also endangers our political independence if the present continentalist policies of the Liberal party and the Conservative party continue to sell our Canada to the foreign corporations.
It is my belief that these needs and challenges, and many more that I do not have time to enumerate, cannot be met by old methods and old approaches. They cannot be met by the 95 large corporations in this country which finance political parties, as is the situation in respect of this government at least, and probably also of those who face them in the Conservative party. They cannot be met by failure to plan. They cannot be met by a Minister of Finance who says he is not prepared to make any forecasts about what will happen to the economy and unemployment. No one in a modern economy has a right to sit in the seat of the Minister of Finance unless he is prepared precisely to plan the economy of the country and attempt to forecast what will happen as a result of the policies he or his predecessor have introduced. This kind of need and challenge cannot be met by the ad hoc policies of LIP or by the Opportunities for Youth program It cannot be met by an attitude of government that every

time there is a problem the solution is to spend more hundreds of millions of dollars and give those hundreds of millions of dollars to the corporations which failed before and whose hope of succeeding now has no basis except the friendliness which the Liberal party has for the 95 corporations.
These needs and challenges cannot be met unless governments are prepared to plan the economy, have the courage to curb the power of the corporations in the land and have the determination to equalize the opportunities for Canadians across Canada. These needs and challenges cannot be met unless governments have the moral initiative to reform the tax system so that the tax burden on the low and middle income groups is removed or at least reduced; unless governments are ready to see that in a modern economy the fate of the country and the fate of the people, the priorities of the country and the priorities of the people and the problems of the country and the problems of the people are not left to private corporations which are answerable only to their shareholders and themselves and not to the people of Canada and the people of the world.
Therefore, I suggest that if we are to have a policy of full employment in this country, a policy to which my party has been committed from the first day, the governments, both federal and provincial, must become more heavily involved in economic planning by using their powers to direct investment and resources to meet social needs instead of the way investment is now being made. That planning must also seek to make Canada competitive in international markets so that job-creating industries may prosper and create jobs for Canadian workers.
Second, if we are to have a full employment policy, manpower and regional expansion policies must be aimed at long-term development rather than being used as a statistical band-aid to cover up the failures of economic policy by getting people temporarily off the unemployment rolls without giving them real jobs and training them for jobs which are not there. Third, we need to have policies to bring about a substantial reduction in interest rates, particularly for housing and other developments. To expect a wage or salary earner to take a mortgage at over 9 per cent interest I say, as I have said outside the House is criminal in a country as rich as this country is.
We have in this country, finally, immense unfilled needs in the urban centres of Canada which must be met if we are to start reducing the unemployment problem to manageable proportions. Therefore, one of the major components of a full employment policy is a program of low-income housing, urban renewal, municipal infrastructure, urban transportation, anti-pollution and purification plants across the country, centres for the aged in Canada, day-care centres for parents who need a place in which to leave their children while they work, more hospital beds and, even more urgently, chronic care units so that the hospital beds may be released for those who need them, and facilities to assist the disturbed and retarded children, facilities which are now shamefully inadequate for the hundreds of thousands of children who do not have an opportunity.
There should be immediate large-scale tax cuts for middle and low-income families to bring about a signifi-
April 24, 1972

cant increase in demand for goods and services. In order to make up for the loss in revenue by necessary tax cuts to lower-income families, the anti-social tax concessions and depletion allowances given to petroleum and mining corporations should be abolished. They have received enough of this kind of treatment for too many years. They have reaped huge profits at the expense of the Canadian people. The time has come to think of the people of Canada instead.
Because the question of taxes is not mentioned in the motion of the Leader of the Opposition I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended by inserting therein, immediately after the words "Canadian industry," the following words:
"has failed to introduce real reform of the tax system so as to redistribute income and reduce the tax burden on low and middle income groups,"
so, the motion as amended would read:
That because the government has failed to produce measures to create employment, has failed to encourage investment in Canadian industry, has failed to introduce real reform of the tax system so as to redistribute income and reduce the tax burden on low and middle income groups and has caused widespread uncertainty as to its economic programs, this House lacks confidence in the ability of the government to meet the needs and challenges of the seventies.
We have had four years of the complacency and failures of the government following, as I said at another time in this House, the year of the centennial of the creation of Canada as a country, following the hopes and the buoyancy of 1967. I say with broken heart rather than with any glee that the government has failed to live up to the opportunities which were created by 1967, the opportunities which the Prime Minister fooled the Canadian people into thinking the government would be capable of realizing. Mr. Speaker, I agree with the Leader of the Opposition that the government has failed the people of Canada. I merely add that so has the Conservative party throughout its history in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I represent a constituency with the lowest per capita income throughout Canada, I believe it is my duty to take part in the debate on the motion before us in order not only to criticize the government but also to give it helpful suggestions to improve the situation, especially in my area.
The motion blames the government for having failed to produce measures to create employment, failed to encour-
Alleqed Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
age investment in Canadian industry and caused widespread uncertainty.
Mr. Speaker, let us examine very objectively our production possibilities in Canada and let us see whether in the industrial field, it is possible under our present system, to create employment without affecting another field concerning those same industries, namely the flow of production, so as to generate new demand to renew such production and provide steady employment to the labour force.
Mr. Speaker, I should not like to quote figures because it is never interesting for listeners, but I shall refer to the words spoken by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) praising the efficiency of our economic system in the production field, when he stated, during a television program in December, that our gross national product was increasing every year in an extraordinary way. He was then quoting the figures published by Statistics Canada and he was perfectly right.
Therefore, all Canadians-industrialists, farmers, businessmen, shopkeepers-manage every year in spite of unemployment, to increase that production which is obviously intended for human consumption. But such consumption is subject to the condition that consumers have the money, the purchasing power needed to buy the things produced for them.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, there was a time in the history of production when one could rightfully say that production was financing consumption. In those days, the production process was not as modern as it is today, it was not mechanized, and man's muscular strength was used to a greater extent to make the things which were needed. Since then, however, man has put his brain to use and invented machines. There have been improvements in all kinds of areas.
In all sectors of economic activity, manufacturers do not hesitate to dismiss workers when they finally realize that they can obtain absolutely the same results changing something in their production process, whether it be by introducing nothing but a six-inch steel piece in the machine, provided it has been invented. Why? To increase their production, reduce their costs, and market their production on a more competitive basis. You cannot blame them for that!
Progress is here to stay and we should take the necessary steps so that our people and mankind may take advantage of it rather than being victimized by progress.
On a number of occasions, we have suggested in this House various programs to improve our faulty system of production distribution. Such arguments may be laughed at but you should read advertisements in the newspapers. For example, in the first issue of La Presse after the strike, there were 70 pages of advertisements. All kinds of products were advertised and offered to Canadians. They were told: they are all for you at reduced prices, at cut prices, etc. And many Canadian women could admire in shop Windows products offered at reduced prices. But since their pocket-books did not say they could buy, they could only gaze upon those products and go back home sighing and thinking they could use all those things.

April 24, 1972
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
Mr. Speaker, if the Canadian people could buy from a store or a company that needs to improve such or such an area of its production, this would also help the manufacturer who could, as I said earlier, get new orders and have his industry work at full capacity.
Even if all Canadian companies were dependent on social welfare or received all kinds of grants to produce more and more cheaply, the problem would not be solved. We should take the bull by the horns and organize consumption.
So, if the consumer level is inadequate, measures to finance it must necessarily be taken. I don't know when efficient and realistic action will be taken in this field.
The government is now acting, but only in a piecemeal fashion. For instance, the Local Initiatives Program, involving expenditures of $150 to $200 million is a mere drop of water in the ocean. Many municipalities have proved that they had prepared worthwile projects.
A short while ago, the hon. member who spoke before me mentioned all kinds of public works which the public has been requesting for years. He is right and I believe that carrying out public works brings about automatic distribution of buying power, making purchase of consumer goods possible, whereas public works are not consumer goods. They can be used, but not consumed. Therefore, through an increase in the volume of our public works we would be distributing more money by way of salaries, buying power, thus ensuring a greater input of orders to industries, and our economy would expand anew.
In fact, many applications submitted by municipalities or local agencies under the Local Initiatives Program have been rejected.
I have here a letter dated March 14, 1972, from Mr. Chevrier, the assistant in the minister's cabinet, in which he simply replied as follows:
This replies to your letter of February 25 concerning project 212-788-Corporation of the Village of Saint-Anselme. We are sorry to inform you that the project has not been accepted by our department.
As you certainly know, this program aroused great interest throughout the country, and we received over 13,000 applications.
They received 13,000 applications because there were 13,000 areas of need. All 13,000 applications were not answered. I go on quoting:
Among the great number of valid applications, we had to choose carefully, taking into account the criteria you know of-
-I surely know them-
-and the budget allocated to us.
I do not approve of this too much. If we have to submit to the will of those who control the nation's credit in order to grant permission and to execute certain projects, I do not agree. The letter goes on:
For those same reasons, a number of valid projects like yours will not receive financial assistance from our department.
Like several other members of this House, I talked on several occasions to the various ministers concerned to ask them to give the Minister of Manpower and Immigra-

tion (Mr. Mackasey), who is responsible for this program, additional funds which would allow him to accept a greater number of valid projects from municipalities, such as the building of sewage systems, culverts, municipal parking lots, or community halls. All those projects are stalled through lack of funds.
Mr. Speaker, if we get a little closer to the immediate, we see that they are now considering applications under another Opportunities for Youth program, and in a communique that the minister has sent us, it is said that 19,000 have been received. This means that young people are prepared to stop, think and prepare projects enabling them not only to earn a few dollars during the summer holidays, in order to get back to college next fall, but to get involved with community life; they are prepared to assume responsibilities, to prove to us that we did not bring them into the world for nothing, in short, they are ready to undertake something.
But concerning these 19,000 applications, to my great surprise, I received recently a communique saying that about 3,000 will be accepted; so, 16,000 will remain. This number, in my view, is far too high. If 16,000 were accepted and 3,000 discarded, I would then say that at least considerable efforts have been made. But in view of the figures that we have been given and because they say that they lack money, I do not agree. I cannot believe in such reasoning because, in a way, such credits are nothing more than figures. When you look for these credits elsewhere, you only bring back figures. Then they will make us the following reproach: those well-known Social Credit party members do talk a lot about credit, they do talk often about money. Mr. Speaker, who does not talk about them?
Everyday in the private sector we can see banks welcoming customers who want short or long term credit. They borrow from a caisse populaire thus they get credit. Then, everyone talks about credit, but it is rather a debt credit. This is acceptable in the private sector because if you lend to a Canadian some of the money you earned you only lend him the product of your work.
But when it comes to Canada being compelled to kowtow to those who forge figures, who demonstrate the credit in Canada, who happen to mint the credit, the products and the work of Canadians, there I do not agree.
It is this credit indebtedness that we are opposing and we would like, at last, to see in Canada a credit system that would be of effective service to the people. This is why Major Douglas in his reform philosophy spoke of social credit since that sort of credit would benefit society.
Mr. Speaker, I have perused several reports in the last few weeks. I am going to comment on what I am conversant with and not on something I do not know. I have noted that in Quebec, the forest industry is in a sad state. Trees are chopped down as if we were the last generation, as if none would follow us, as if the world would end there and then, when it is a fact that the end is not yet in sight and that we should develop our national resources in such a way as to ensure not only their permanence but their increase.
I had then suggested that during the summer holidays young and willing people should be sent to work and
April 24, 1972

make the forests grow. This would create jobs they could fill and come to like; they would live in harmony with nature and discover what our natural resources are. And instead of only sowing the seeds of discontent in their hearts, we would teach them to love their country.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to see how we fail sometimes to shoulder our responsibilities and that some of our leaders behave irresponsibly, availing themselves of a difficult situation to exploit violence and train the young to bring down our institutions.
I once met a group of young people and told them that instead of bringing down everything, they should find out where the deficiency lies and the reason why they are unable to develop in a normal way.
I also gave them the following comparison: Suppose we are in a house in which the temperature is only 55 degrees, while it is 30 degrees outside; 55 degrees inside is not particularly comfortable-it makes us shiver. So we first notice that we are not comfortable because the heating is defective. Well, somebody decides to stir up all the people there, to convince them to demonstrate and break the windows. Do you think it is going to be warmer in that room afterwards? They answered: No. It is not by demonstrating or breaking windows that we can solve the problem; we have to get to the bottom of things.
So I told them this: Let us go down to the basement and have a look at the heating installation so we can find out where the defect lies, and once we have discovered whether there is power to activate the fan, to activate the pump, we may discover that the furnace is in good condition, but the oil only comes drop by drop-and the furnace can only burn whatever oil it gets. So let us check the oil pipe to find out where the defect is.
Through checking this, we end up in our neighbor's basement, and there, we inquire from him and learn that he is in the same situation. We follow up along the oil pipe which feeds the furnaces in the third and fourth houses, and find that the situation is the same everywhere.
At one point, we discover that an invisible control regulates the oil supply to all the furnaces, and that there lies the cause of the trouble.
So I told them that instead of breaking windows they should air their grievance against the invisible hand preventing oil from reaching burners which would enable furnaces to function and to satisfy everybody.
Mr. Speaker, these -young people understood me very well. I wanted them to get to the core of things so as to speak against what prevents us from living a normal life, not to destroy the social structure, the society which our forefathers have succeeded in erecting but in improving the structure by adding another story which would give them room to have their place within security and freedom.
