speechtext:
Canada, as the world's fifth largest exporting nation, depends for much of its prosperity and employment on the state of world markets. Everyone knows this; yet opposition critics talk as if the state of the world is the government's fault. This is utter nonsense. The fact is that this world of ours has been through an extremely difficult period in the past five or six years. Perhaps not since the great depression have there been so many economic challenges for the nations of the world to meet. Yet, as the Financial Times of London says:
Canada's industrial output has risen faster and prices have risen slower than in any other democratic country on the face of the earth.
Yet, the opposition tells us that it is ashamed of this kind of economic performance. It is to the credit of the Canadian people that, despite the attacks we have heard from the other side, this goal has been reached. The barrage of criticism continues. They said, "Why haven't you solved unemployment," and, "Why does inflation continue?"
I should like to say something about unemployment. The Leader of Her Majesty's Official Opposition spoke about a plan for more employment. However, that is a plan which he carefully concealed from the people of Nova Scotia during the years when he was prime minister of that province. The present record of job creation in this country makes his Nova Scotia statistics look abysmal in comparison. There are questions asked about unemployment and inflation which cannot be answered by the Government of Canada alone. The Government of Canada, as the Leader of the Opposition well knows, possesses no bank of levers which can be pulled in some sort of miraculous sequence and achieve, simultaneously, full employment, stable prices and unbounded industrial expansion. That can come about only through co-operation between governments at all levels and with the private sector.
We know that provincial governments, in conjunction with their municipalities, collect more money and spend more money than does the federal government. Only through co-operative efforts by governments at all levels, the private sector, trade unions, agriculture and so on, can we meet our economic goals. While we still have some distance to travel toward those goals, and other speakers will deal with the economic aspects of this resolution later, this country of ours, despite the blue ruin gang, has been doing much better than anyone thought we could. In fact, our economy has been growing at a fantastic clip. It has been growing at a rate twice as fast as that of the United States. In fact, it has been outstripping the United States ever since the present Prime Minister assumed office in 1968. In March, 8,016,000 Canadians were working. Between 97 and 98 per cent of heads of families were working. Unfortunately, some are not working. For them,

this represents a real tragedy. We have to work together co-operatively in our society to provide opportunities for them. There are 336,000 more Canadians working than one year ago. This is the highest growth rate of any industrial country in the western world.
We face some unique challenges. In its fourth annual report, the Economic Council of Canada told us that in the 15 year period beginning in 1965 and ending in 1980, the Canadian labour force would grow by 50 per cent. This is an incredible growth rate, a growth rate entirely unique in the western world. The need to provide this number of jobs is the challenge and the opportunity which all of us have, whether we work in government at the local, provincial or federal level, or whether we are associated with private industry, trade unions or the agricultural community.
Let us compare the growth in our work force with that of other countries. The United States labour force is to grow by 30 per cent against our 50 per cent for Canada; the United Kingdom 4.5 per cent in the same 15 years; Sweden a zero growth rate and France, a 13.5 per cent increase by 1980. In Germany, the predicted growth rate of the labour force in this period is 5.5 per cent. In Italy, the rate is 2.5 per cent. In Canada, I repeat, it is 50 per cent. It has been said before that this is an historic, nonrecurring opportunity and challenge for the people of this country, because if we can get an economy that will put these people to work, and they are mostly young people, relatively well educated, we are going to have in this country an economic base for a more just society and those greater opportunities that we all want in areas other than the economic area.
What is this rate in real terms? In real terms, the challenge is quite staggering. We will be adding three million people to the labour force in that 15 year period. In the first five year period from 1965 to 1970, one million new jobs were created in Canada. That is a remarkably good record. The three million people who will come into the Canadian labour force by 1980 will equal the absolute additions of people to the labour forces of Great Britain, West Germany and Italy combined in that period. With our population based on 22 million people, we have to find as many jobs as those three countries combined. That is a very significant challenge.
Despite these facts, the opposition thrashes about trying to convert every sign of progress into evidence of impending catastrophe. These Jeremiahs among us carefully conceal these facts from the Canadian public; in the first five years of the period about which the Economic Council advised us, over 1.2 million new jobs were created in Canada. This total of more than one million equals the new jobs created in seven European countries; Great Britain, France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, Sweden and the Netherlands. There are 22 million people in Canada and 200 million in Europe, yet the critics blast ahead-we heard them again today-and suggest that somehow Canada's economic performance has been inadequate or suffers in comparison with some of the other countries of the world.
While the growth rate of Canada's labour force is six times that of western European countries and twice as fast as that of the United States, we continue to hear
April 24, 1972

criticism in this House. I would like the members of the opposition to call the following statements to mind. Perhaps they would like to explain them to the Canadian people. We have heard accusations in this House that the government is responsible for the rate of inflation, despite the fact it is the lowest of 22 nations in the western world. The socialist leader who today calls for full employment in a more candid moment, when speaking to an NDP council meeting in Ottawa on September 21, 1970, said and I quote:
It is politically impossible for the NDP in its present position to say full employment and we don't care where prices go!
That is an admission by the leader of the New Democratic Party that a price has to be paid for inflation, whatever that price may be. The official opposition has expressed similar concerns. Today, they lecture us about our alleged sins of omission and commission. Yet, the official finance spokesman for that party stated before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs on November 4, 1969, and I quote:
I am just as concerned as you are-I think all members of the House are-about the problem of inflation, and I think our chief concern is not so much to suggest that what you are doing is wrong, but that we fear that some of the things you may be doing are wrong, so that we miss the boat.
That is what the Conservative party told parliament and Canada in 1969. The official spokesman continued:
If the national effort results in an underkill on this score it will be far worse than the overkill; because if we have a national underkill in this fight against inflation we will have to start all over, and I think the square of zero is going to be much further back again. This is what bothers me.
Those were the words of the official spokesman for the official opposition concurring in the fight against inflation. But now, when these opposition parties discover there is some political fallout, that a price is being paid because of a failure of segments of the Canadian society to heed the request of the Prime Minister of this country for voluntary restraints, they say, "there is nobody in this economic chicken house but us chickens". They refuse to acknowledge any previous attitude at all which would have supported that fight against inflation. It is difficult to believe today that these two masters of hindsight would ever have uttered words which admitted that a price had been paid for inflation. Let the House and the Canadian people know that the government shares a real concern for inflation and the danger of pricing Canadian goods out of international markets. Despite these difficult months, Canadians have every right to feel proud of what has been done, and more remains.
What does the challenge to create more jobs mean for government? It means that in addition to normal fiscal and monetary measures designed to stimulate employment, we must adopt measures of an extraordinary kind to provide employment opportunities, especially for the thousands of people coming into the work force. The Department of Manpower and Immigration is deeply concerned about this challenge to provide more jobs. The resolution suggests current programs and services do not go far enough in meeting the needs of Canadians, particularly the working poor, displaced people and young
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
people in search of employment. The facts do not support the allegations in the resolution.
The services of the Department of Manpower and Immigration have included extensive and well financed programs to provide labour market information and analysis, employment counselling and career guidance, job matching and placement services, adult training programs which include "in-industry" and "on-the-job" training programs, manpower adjustment services in cases of technological and industrial change and special programs for certain groups in the labour force, especially the disadvantaged.
Certain opposition spokesmen made reference to the challenge involved in finding employment for students and young people, yet opposition representatives must be aware of the fact that a summer employment program for students has been operated for some years by our Canada Manpower Centres. During the last four summers, the department initiated special efforts and programs to help students find summer jobs. Based on the experience of the past few years, it is estimated that 1,306,000 students will be seeking employment this summer; 434,000 postsecondary and 872,000 secondary. This represents an increase of 114,000 over 1970; 41,000 post secondary and 73,000 secondary.
In 1972, the Department of Manpower and Immigration will generally conduct the same activities as in 1971, with the following changes: one, the number of CM Centres for students will be increased from 119 to 137; two, an interregional, student summer employment program will be introduced whereby up to 2,000 post-secondary students will be provided with an opportunity to obtain employment during the summer months in regions or provinces other than the ones in which they reside and would normally work.
In October, 1971, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration was given responsibility for the execution of the special employment plan. This is a direct expenditure and loan program in the amount of $465 million, concentrated, to the extent possible, in the period October, 1971, to May 31, 1972. It consists of an employment loan program providing $160 million to the provinces, a $10 million loan program for exhibitions and fairs, a local initiatives program of $150 million, and an additional manpower retraining program of $65 million.
The local initiatives program was designed to provide the greatest possible good to Canadian communities while putting the largest number of people to work. It enabled municipalities, community organizations and private groups to submit labour-intensive projects for approval and funding. Of the $150 million allotted to the program, $50 million was made available to municipalities across Canada in consultation with provincial governments. The balance was available for projects submitted by community organizations and private groups. Over 5,600 projects were approved under this program, creating 90,000 jobs. So much for the prediction of the opposition that no more than 50,000 jobs would be created.
The Canadian manpower training-on-the-job program was introduced as one of the 1971-72 winter special

April 24, 1972
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
employment programs. It was designed to stimulate employers to prepare for future economic expansion and permit persons who would otherwise be unemployed to learn on-the-job skills which will be of continuous value to them by increasing their employability or earning capacity and by preparing them to take advantage of future employment opportunities. The department has entered into approximately 12,000 contracts with employers to the value of $50 million to train some 41,000 trainees at an average cost of $1200 for an average training period of 17 weeks. Yet the leader of the socialist party stands in his place and attacks this program as one which does not train people for jobs which are available. It was a ridiculous and unworthy statement by a man who aspires to be prime minister of this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this government, together with the administration which held office during the Pearson years, has had nine years in which to plan and produce in the interests of all the citizens in our country. It is now clear that these Liberal years have been poor ones for the many and lucrative ones for the few, particularly for Liberals who are Liberal in name only and who are hogging the benefits of power for themselves and their 'in' clique.
Today, after four years of gross mismanagement of the economy and chaos in practically every government department, we charge and can prove that the government has failed to provide measures to create sufficient employment. We can, with even greater force, charge and prove that it knew there would be a great influx of young people on the labour market in the 'sixties-the post-war crop-and that it has utterly failed to plan and provide jobs in their interest. They have been neglected while over-emphasis was placed, and time and money were wasted on constitutional vagaries, rule changes, international intrigue, government shuffles, Information Canada and trips abroad.

Our young people have been ignored while the ceiling on interest rates was lifted and an 11 per cent tax placed on building materials to make their entry into their life work-pattern even more difficult. Mr. Speaker, if we are to solve our problems of unemployment and inflation, the present mismanagement of our economy by this government must be brought to a halt. The statement that our economy has been mismanaged is an indisputable fact which can easily be verified by glancing at a few statistics.
The rate of capital investment is down from 11 per cent last year to a projected 5 per cent this year. During the years 1968-71 the annual average seasonally-adjusted unemployment rate was 5.5 per cent per year. This stands in sharp contrast to the years 1964-67 when the rate was 4.1 per cent. And now, ominously, in March of this year it reached 6 per cent. Furthermore, since 1967 the gap between the actual and potential levels of the gross national product in constant dollars has widened considerably, reaching around 4 per cent in 1970. This represents a gap of approximately $3 billion in 1970. The rate of real economic growth last year dropped to 3.3 per cent from 5.1 per cent in 1969, in comparison to the potential growth rate of 5.5 per cent. In other words, Mr. Speaker, our levels of output and income would have been considerably greater with reasonably full use of Canada's labour force and other productive resources. Therefore, changes must be made. Perhaps the most beneficial of the possible changes would be the introduction of full employment budgeting techniques.
The Ontario budget plan for 1971-72 used the full-employment budgeting approach for the first time by any government in Canada in the design of fiscal policy. Full-employment budgeting is now being used by the United States federal government. Full-employment budgeting is particularly relevant to the current economic situation and the problem of fiscal policy co-ordination in the Canadian federal system. Budgetary deficits are commonly understood to be expansionary. However, the full-employment budget adds a new dimension to this conventional approach to fiscal policy formulation. It emphasizes the way in which revenues increase as economic activity revives and exert a "tax drag", thereby slowing down economic expansion possibly before full employment has been achieved. The intention in such budgeting procedures is to offset any slack in the economy, and counteract the government's loss of tax revenue by cutting taxes in such a way that the growth potential of the economy is restored. On balance, these changes should reduce the expansionary impact of the tax cuts and discretionary expenditure increases.
Thus, in comparison with federal fiscal policy in 197172, three features of Ontario policy stand out. First, it was based on an objective "full employment budgeting" assessment of the impact of current policy. Second, it included more emphasis on tax cuts rather than expenditure increases. We must bear in mind that the expenditure of the federal government this year is being increased by 23 per cent. In addition, those increases in expenditures that occurred were mainly direct, rather than arm's length. Third, the major policy incentives-tax credits and
April 24, 1972

cuts, and winter employment expenditure programs- preceded similar federal action.
I should like now to say something about the problems of designing and implementing short-term economic stabilization policy. The task of short-term economic stabilization is demonstrably very difficult. It is, however, even more complicated in a federal state such as Canada. Nevertheless, in light of the obvious failure of federal policies to maintain high levels of employment, and in view of the absence of new federal initiatives with respect to federal-provincial fiscal policy co-ordination, it seems important to consider briefly those problems revealed. These are the problems of lags in the implementation of policy changes, the balance of policy mix between expenditure changes and tax changes, and the problem of estimating the direction and degree of fiscal impact.
Even so, the full employment budget estimates show that-on a national accounts basis-the federal fiscal impact was expansionary in 1970, though nowhere nearly sufficient completely to reverse 1969's restrictive impact. In 1971-72, the planned federal expansionary swing is more pronounced, partly because of a carry-over into the current fiscal year of unrealized 1970-71 spending intentions. Some carry-over of this year's program into next year appears inevitable, and it is thus unlikely that the full planned impact will materialize in 1971-72. However, the tax reductions in this year's program give it more flexibility than last year's and there seems to be no reason to doubt that this combined expansionary fiscal impact of 1970-71 and 1971-72 is greater than the restrictive impact of 1969.
Ontario fiscal policy for 1970-71 was, in contrast to federal policy, designed from the outset to be expansionary, albeit moderately so. It showed the same adaptability as federal policy, undergoing substantial in-year changes intended to reinforce its expansionary thrust. Ontario fiscal policy was more flexible than federal policy because in-year changes in expenditures were concentrated in direct rather than arm's length categories. Direct expenditures offer a greater degree of short-term flexibility.
In the past two years the fiscal impact of the Ontario government on the provincial economy has been almost as pronounced, in relative terms, as that of the federal government on the Canadian economy. Accordingly, the Ontario budget has become a key economic document in so far as the short-term economic stabilization of the Ontario economy is concerned. This recent evolution of an independent provincial fiscal policy in Ontario underscores the importance of federal-provincial fiscal policy co-ordination. Over the past two years the direction of thrust in federal and Ontario fiscal policies has, fortunately, been the same. However, independent pursuit of contrary policies is a possibility in the future, given existing evidence of lack of co-ordination.
This year, for example, in the absence of federal plans for dealing with winter employment problems the Ontario government went ahead with its own program. Subsequently, the federal government instituted its program which overlaps the Ontario program in certain areas. Such duplication limits the efficiency and flexibility of fiscal policy in Ontario. There is little doubt that the
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
utilization of federal-provincial fiscal resources could be made more efficient through co-ordinated policies.
The finance committee in the other place has also supported the concept of full employment budgeting in one of its recent reports in these words:
The Minister of Finance told us that he discerned some important practical difficulties in applying a high employment budgeting rule to the Canadian federal government and he questioned whether the concept would be particularly illuminating to the public or otherwise useful.
We took careful account of the minister's views on this point. But we could not help observing also that the Ontario government, as well as the United States federal government, has seen virtue in the concept, and that both have found ways of adapting it to their needs. It seems to us that some reasonably flexible adaptation of the concept to the budgeting of the federal government in Canada would also be helpful.
We therefore recommend that the federal government adopt the concept of high employment budgeting, at least to the extent of always estimating, in budget presentations, what the budgetary position would be at high employment and of analyzing reasons for changes in the estimated figures since the previous presentations.
The needs and challenges of the seventies require new methods of approaching and solving problems. We must not allow our economy to be hamstrung by a government that believes in exercising with dumbbells. We must seek a government that will pay full attention to the main concerns of the Canadian people, particularly in the economic and technological fields.
As I have already shown, the use of full employment budgeting techniques would greatly benefit Canada. Its use would disperse much of the confusion and uncertainty felt in the business community towards the government's economic programs. However, it will still be necessary for this government to stop harassing Canadian commerce and industry with unworkable tax changes. When will we know what amendments are proposed to the 1971 Domesday book? Surely, this uncertainty cannot be permitted to go on and on, to the detriment of investment in Canadian industry and confidence in Canada.
The sudden ad hoc introductions of the Opportunities for Youth program and the local initiatives program are evidence of the government's failure to create sufficient employment through the stimulation of the private sector of the Canadian economy and particularly Canadian industry. Canadian job-creating enterprises in the private sector must be developed, encouraged and assisted by government so that Canadian taxpayers' dollars will no longer be used on hastily conceived programs that yield little or no long-term benefits. I am thinking particularly, of course, of our experience with much of the hot and cold LIP program which is now apparently going to be entrenched and run year round by this incompetent, welfare-state government.
Because the government has failed to produce measures to create employment, has failed to encourage investment in Canadian industry and has caused widespread uncertainty as to its economic program and, indeed, has failed to introduce real reform in the tax system so as to redistribute income and reduce the tax burden on the low and middle income groups, this House lacks confidence or

April 24, 1972
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
certainly should in the ability of the government to meet the needs and challenges of the 1970's. What we have experienced in the sixties we certainly must not put up with in the seventies.

Mr. Speaker, I have enjoyed this debate today, if only because it has become familiar. Things familiar sometimes become enjoyable. I have heard what was said today so many times before I know the lines before they are spoken. I read recently that a California newspaper had tried to stay in business by reporting only the happy events that occurred in the world, but the newspaper went broke. Many other newspapers in the world have illustrated the fact that you cannot make a living by reporting only good news. The fellows who are competing with you are busy reporting all the bad news in the country, because they think they can make a living this way. That is the way the opposition are trying to make a living.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) goes around the country ringing his hands over and over again. He is gaining the reputation as being the man who makes people in Canada sad. We have people in Canada, such as Wayne and Shuster, who make a good living as comedians. For the first time in history, we have a man going around the country making people sad, and making a living very well by doing that.
I was interested in some of the statistics given so far during this debate, particularly those given a minute ago by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Ryan). I realize his speech was prepared by the Conservative party research staff, but I think that even they should use correct figures. The hon. member mentioned, for instance, real growth last year. As he wrung his hands he said real growth last year dropped to 3.1 per cent in Canada. Let me give you the correct figures. Real growth in Canada rose from 3.3 per cent in 1970 to 5.4 per cent last year. I suppose if one wrings his hands long enough he can turn the figures around, get them backwards, and make the picture look bad. I think it is encumbent upon spokesmen for the Conservative party in this House to use the correct figures, and it is encumbent upon the leader of the opposition party to hire a staff capable of securing the correct figures.
What about figures in respect of unemployment? These were very adequately stated by the hon. member for Bur-naby-Seymour (Mr. Perrault), who talked about the real growth in employment in Canada. We have an outstanding record in Canada in job creation in that some 330,000 new jobs were developed in Canada last year. This is a much better record than that of Italy, France and West Germany combined. Our employment growth rate was twice that of the United States, and six times the rate of those European countries I mentioned. Is that a record of which to be ashamed? I am not ashamed of that record. It is the greatest record of job production in any country of the world. There is a saying in the stock markets that bad money drives out good money. I know the Leader of the Opposition will drive out good news. We have to correct these statements over and over again in Canada in order to contradict the doom and pessimism given out day after 
day by the Conservative party in Canada. That party is trying to destroy the confidence of Canadians in their country.
We have an outstanding record in many fields, including the field of inflation fighting in Canada. Let me refer to figures to which the doom and gloom boys fail to pay attention. The figures issued by the international monetary fund, not by us, show that last year in Canada the amount of inflation was 3.5 per cent, as compared to 9.9 per cent in Britain, 5.5 per cent in France, 5.7 per cent in Germany, 5.3 per cent in Norway, 4.2 per cent in the United States and 9.7 per cent in Japan. Canada's record is 3.5 per cent, the best in the world. Tell me any country which can do better than that.
We have the highest rate of employment in the world. The reason Canadians have trouble finding jobs is that we have more people coming into the labour force than any other country in the world. That is not a record of which we should be ashamed. We have a great and growing nation. We will have problems for a good many years to come because there are so many Canadians coming into the labour market, but we should be very grateful for this growth rate. We will not help the problem by expressing lack of confidence day after day as has been done by the Leader of the Opposition.
The hon. member for Spadina referred to the rate of capital investment as being 5 per cent this year. He read us a long treatise on economics. He mentioned the lag factor, but he needs to know more about the lag factor and the rate of capital investment. This is exactly what took place in respect of the 5 per cent figure last year. The long-term average is about 6 per cent in Canada, and the indications are that our long-term average has in fact been far above the 5 per cent figure in recent years. Canada has a very commendable record in respect of the rate of capital investment.
Let me refer to something said by the leader of the NDP. He referred to secondary indicators in Canada as being down, but he did not quote his sources. I could quote them for him because this story has appeared recently in newspaper articles all across the country. This newspaper article was wrong, so the source of the leader of the NDP was wrong, as usual.
The suggestion has been made that manufacturing shipments declined in February after advancing in January. Manufacturing shipments were down in February but this followed an unusually rapid advance in January. The trend of any statistical series fluctuates from month to month. Manufacturing shipments have been rising strongly for more than a year. Manufacturing shipments in February 1972 were nearly 12 per cent higher than in the same month in 1971. The doom and gloom boys on the other side will not pay attention to the good figures. They look under as many rocks as they can to see what they can find to show that things are not good in Canada.
A comment was made about manufacturers' inventories, suggesting that they grew in relation to shipments of newly finished goods. I suggest that is just boloney. The comment in respect of the increase of manufacturers' inventories in relation to shipments is simply not justified. The stock to shipments ratio in 1972 was 1.9, the same as in the last three months, and this ratio is lower than in any three month period during the last three years. In fact, the
April 24, 1972

stock to shipments ratio is usually low by historic standards, but the doom and gloom boys will not pay any attention to these figures.
Then, we have another one. Figures released a few days ago by Statistics Canada showed that the index of industrial production, which increased slightly in January, has been falling since the first of the year. This statement is in error, because the truth is that the index of industrial production, which represents about one third of the total output of the Canadian economy, rose at a seasonally adjusted rate of about 4 per cent as at January, 1972, following an exceptionally rapid increase of more than 10 per cent in December, 1971. Those are the figures the people on the other side should be quoting. There is a practice in Canada that a speaker is sometimes led into a meeting by the bagpipes. Sometimes he is led in to the tune of a spritely march. I am told now that when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) is led in by the bagpipes, the piper plays a lament.
I wish to say something about the claim made by the Leader of the New Democratic Party that this government deliberately created unemployment. That has been said over and over again by the gloom boys on the other side.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Perrault), and the other member also, spoke of the Conservative gloom and doom, I thought I should let them know I have seen
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
gloom and doom in my riding. I wish the Liberal workers in my riding in the last election had been here to hear these gentlemen opposite who have spoken, because quite a number of them today are on welfare as a result of the policies of this Liberal government. The hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour spoke about what will happen 15 years from now. This statement is similar to one made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in Toronto a few weeks ago when he referred to what would happen a decade from now in the north. It is a well known fact that his speech was a re-hash of the speech he heard from a former Conservative Prime Minister concerning visions of the north. Instead of mentioning what will happen in the next decade, members opposite should be telling us what will happen now. I think they should take a lesson from the slogan of Manpower-do it now, and not 10 or 15 years from now.
In 1965, unemployment was as low as 3.6 per cent. In 1968 when this government came to power, unemployment ran between 4 and 5 per cent and hence to 8.1 per cent in February of 1971. There were 675,000 Canadians out of work and about 100,000 undergoing manpower training, which actually meant 775,000 were out of work. This government diddled with they called a seasonally adjusted formula to make the figures look lower than they actually were. This high unemployment was deliberately caused by a government policy to curb inflation. The Liberals called it an all-out war on inflation. This war caused many to go on welfare. The people of Canada demanded wage and price controls. This is substantiated by various questionnaires sent out by members of parliament, including myself. The government chose to cause unemployment as a cure for inflation, and at the same time caused more inflation by allowing bank interest rates to go up to 11 and 12 per cent. While the Liberal government ran on a ticket of Canadian unity, the just society, and a prosperous economy, it has done more to divide and to segregate than any other government, through a planned deliberate policy to create unemployment, the root of all evil.
This government has given fuel to such activists as Mel Watkins and Jim Laxer and their communist manifesto, and to those who agree on Quebec separating as long as Quebec would become a socialistic state. It has also provided fuel for Pierre Bourgeault, Chartrand, Laberge and Rene Levesque, who have now reinforced their manifesto for separation. In the 1960's Jean Lesage's "Maitre chez Nous" slogan created a situation in which the Bour-geaults, the Chartrands, Laberges and the Levesques, who are determined to make a separate state of Quebec, perpetuated slogans such as: anti-federalism, anti-the Queen, anti-Americanism, anti-establishment, anti-free enterprise, anti-Viet Nam, anti-management, anti-Anglais and so on. And now we have the Levesque manifesto, a formula to separate the province of Quebec and make it a socialistic, sovereign state. Men like Levesque, Bourgeault, Laberge, Chartrand, Laxer and Watkins scare the hell out of the industrialists who want to expand their industries in Canada and scare the hell out of those who want to create new ones, whether they are foreign owned, American or even Canadian, and add to the causes of unemployment.

April 24, 1972
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
In the past four years, instead of going in the direction of unity the Liberals and NDP have created a situation in which Canadian nationalism has become anti-American and anti-foreign investment. This is now part and parcel of a Canadian form of patriotism, a form of Canadian maitre chez nous. They felt that a strong sense of federal nationalism would lessen the centrifugal tendencies in the country and would tear down provincialism. Such negation is a somewhat weak basis for national sentiment to focus upon and Canadians have become concerned about the varying shades of nationalism which have been advanced over the past few years. John Deutsch, former chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, feels that there is no country where the blind furies of nationalism could be more dangerous than Canada in the 1970s. He contends that exploitation of this sentiment could destroy Canada. The Liberal party is just doing that, and this is one of the main reasons why I could not follow them.
The government has no information as to how many Canadians own property in the U.S.A., no information as to how many own businesses in the U.S.A., and no information as to how many own stock in the U.S.A. and its worth. The government has no decisive evidence about the costs and benefits of foreign investment in the Canadian economy. The story is told of a Canadian computer company that was unable to find risk capital in Canada. It is now 70 per cent owned in the U.S.A. Would it have been better for Canada if that firm had been allowed to fail- better dead than American? Whatever the origin of capital, such a firm provides employment and income for Canadians the same as all other businesses.
President Nixon, in his statement to the House on April 14, gave an assurance that he will not stand in the way when Canada charts its on own economic course. The point is, what economic course are we taking? In what direction are we going? No policy has been announced by the government. If it is to be a policy of anti-American ownership and investment, the President will be happy because he will have an opportunity to retain that capital in the U.S.A. and expand industry and employment in his own country while we look for capital-where?
Canadians are not oriented to investing directly in corporate stock, nor has the CDC any intention of so orienting them. I point out that I asked the former minister of finance that this be done by the CDC in order to orient Canadians to invest in Canadian industry from childhood through adult life. Is the government going to continue to create an atmosphere of anti-American, anti-foreign investment and at the same time bribe industry to establish in designated areas and bribe youth to do their own thing because the government has failed to restore confidence in the country, has failed to expand our economy and create jobs and has deliberately created this mess?
I will definitely vote for the motion of no-confidence proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) which reads as follows:
That because the government has failed to produce measures to create employment, has failed to encourage investment in Canadian industry, and has caused widespread uncertainty as to its economic programs, this House lacks confidence in the ability of the government to meet the needs and challenges of the seventies.

In 1968, Mr. Speaker, as a Liberal I campaigned for a working majority in parliament. In the next election, as a Conservative I will campaign for a majority working.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the latest public opinion poll taken by the Canadian Institute of Public Opinion shows that 41 per cent of the people polled believe that unemployment is Canada's most serious problem. Just a few years ago, in 1966, when the same question was asked only 7 per cent of the Canadian people thought unemployment was the most serious problem.
I listened to the two parliamentary secretaries who have spoken on behalf of the government and heard them say that there is really no problem about unemployment, that the Canadian people really are not upset about unemployment, that things are really going well in this country and that the only trouble is that members of the opposition parties are using spurious arguments to excite the Canadian people about the dangers of unemployment. I say to the parliamentary secretaries that they give a great deal more credit than can be given to any group when they suggest that members of the opposition parties have been whipping up the present feeling about unemployment. That feeling is not based on the speeches of members of the opposition; it is based on the cold hard realities of what is taking place.
It will do little good for parliamentary secretaries, or for the minister who is going to speak tonight on behalf of the government, to tell us about how good they think things are, that many more people are working in Canada than ever before and all the rest of the goodies. For the more than 600,000 who are unemployed it is cold comfort to be told that somebody else never had it better than it is at present.
What are the facts? It is the facts we should be examining, not the fables we get from the government side. Last month there were 642,000 people out of work, an increase of 15,000 over February. The seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment stood at exactly 6 per cent. Mr. Speaker, in the last 22 or 23 months, in only one month has the seasonally adjusted rate of unemployment been less than 6 per cent. I want to put on record again that the average number of people unemployed in every month during the four years in which the Trudeau government has been in office is exactly twice as many as in all the months in the four years in which the Pearson government was in office. That is the record of the Trudeau government.
If you look at it region by region, the situation is even more grim. In the Atlantic region, the actual rate of unemployment in March stood at 12.1 per cent, up from 11.1 per cent in February and 10.9 per cent in March of last year. In British Columbia, one of our wealthiest provinces, the actual unemployment rate jumped from 7.6 per cent in February to 8.6 per cent in March. I do not know why the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Perrault) is so happy about things when the situation in British Columbia shows such a large number of unemployed.

That is true, and we have never questioned that this would be the result of the government's policy. While we have the lowest increase in the cost of living, we also have the highest rate of unemployment of any industrial-

ized country. In December, 1969, when asked by the press how serious he was about dealing with inflation, the Prime Minister said, "Just watch us. We will follow these policies to curb inflation even if they result in an unemployment rate of 6 per cent."

Is it any wonder that members of the opposition, the public, the academic economists and those who work with people on welfare say that this government is callous, that it is indifferent and that it does not care about people who are unemployed? Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
Mr. Speaker, let me digress from Mrs. Cohen's article for a moment in order to remind members of the House that the figures collected by Statistics Canada and the Department of Manpower and Immigration make a mockery of the statement which the Prime Minister has made a number of times, that people who want work can get work. The amendment says that the government "has failed to introduce real reform of the tax system so as to redistribute income and reduce the tax burden on low and middle income groups." I do not want today to go over the mass of material prepared by the hon. member for Duvernay, which shows that certain industries, oil and gas for example, and the mining industry are paying taxes on only 10 per cent of earned income, that other industries pay more and that individuals pay tax usually on their whole income.
The Prime Minister has repeatedly made speeches in which he has put forward the argument that the objective

of the government is to narrow the gap between Canadians in the lower income bracket and those in the upper income bracket. Again and again the Prime Minister has said that the government is succeeding in its objective. The facts prove differently. Hon. members may have seen, in the Financial Times, a report of speeches made at a conference organized by the Canadian Council for Social Development by two United States economists. The speeches deal with Canada and use figures prepared by Statistics Canada and the Department of National Revenue. These are the same as the figures which I obtained in answer to questions I recently put on the order paper.
The figures show that between 1957 and 1967, the lowest 40 per cent of families and individuals in Canada who paid taxes earned under 16 per cent of the total income. In other words, the lowest 40 per cent got less than 16 per cent of total income. Actually, Mr. Speaker, the percentage of total income earned by the lowest 40 per cent, instead of going up as the Prime Minister seems to have indicated in a number of speeches, has gone down. At the same time, the percentage earned by the top 40 per cent has gone up slightly. The top 40 per cent of income earners in this country in 1967, the last year for which there are figures, earned 66.6 per cent of the total income. In other words, the top 40 per cent got two-thirds of the income earned by Canadians. The answer to another question which I asked shows what has happened in this area. Hon. members can see the answer to this question in Hansard of March 29.
I want to make it clear that I cannot put all the figures on record. The number of taxpayers increased between 1961 and 1969 by about 60 per cent. However, if you look at the number of people earning income of over $200,000 a year, you will see that the number doubled from 95 to 190. The minister from Calgary smiles; he does not think that is very many. Those who are unemployed or who earn an income of less than $5,000 a year, which includes almost half the people of this country, think if anybody is earning over $200,000 a year it is a lot of people.
In the period 1961-69, the number of people earning between $100,000 and $200,000 tripled from 507 to 1,553. The number of people earning between $25,000 and $100,000 increased by 3i times, from 18,730 to 68,570. So, Mr. Speaker, one can see that under this Liberal government which has introduced a certain tax system but has refused to implement a truly equitable tax system, those who have most are getting more than ever before. Not only is the income growing of those in the top earnings bracket, but the number receiving a large income is also growing. At the same time, almost half the population still earns less than $5,000 per year.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before six o'clock, I had just a few moments to deal with the premise on which the amendment proposed by the hon. member for York South is based, that is, the suggestion that we as a government have not introduced tax reform and that the effect of whatever we have done has not been of assistance to the lower and middle income groups. This is a subject on which I could spend the whole of my allotted time. However, I do not propose to get trapped into doing that.
I have dealt with the fact that a great number of taxpayers in Canada have been relieved, either wholly or in part, of taxation as a result of Bill C-259 that was dealt with in the last session of this parliament. I could mention such things as the employment expense allowance and the child-care allowance that are of primary interest and benefit to lower and middle income wage earners in Canada. I could dwell at length on the additional exemption that our senior citizens receive, the change that resulted in the increase from $500 to $650 and the age for qualification being reduced from 70 to 65. These are all
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
things that are well recognized in Canada. Lower and middle income Canadians know that today they are paying less tax under the reformed Income Tax Act than before, because since the first of the year the deductions from their pay envelopes have been smaller.
The hon. member said we have not reformed the tax system. He may not like the reform: that is beside the point. How he can deny it is reform escapes me completely. It altered fundamentally the basis on which small Canadian corporations are assisted through the tax system. It changed significantly the way corporations and their shareholders are taxed. It permitted and encouraged Canadians to set aside substantially more tax free and tax deferred dollars for their retirement. It increased both the number and effectiveness of incentives for Canadians to invest in and own Canadian enterprise. It attached very definite and positive conditions to the tax incentives available to the extractive industries. It instituted for the first time the inclusion of capital gains in the tax base and abolished federal gift and estate taxes.
That may not be reform by the standards of the socialists who feel that not only is a buck a buck but it is the government's buck. It is, and was, reform by any rational standard of definition. It was founded on an unprecedented process of participation, a process of good democracy, good politics and good government. The tax reform which this government introduced and saw carried through the House of Commons in the last session was responsible reform.
Those who were present in the House just before six o'clock when I started my address will appreciate that I was feeling something in the position of making my maiden speech. I blew my opening lines beautifully. This is the first occasion I have had as a member of the ministry to take part in a debate on behalf of the government. After listening to the speech of the leader of the opposition when introducing his motion today, I felt like a Conservative, at least as I understand many Conservatives feel: I was let down and disappointed.
Most Canadians are well aware of the fact that in our parliamentary system opposition parties have a vitally important role to play. The opposition has a responsibility to oppose, but it also has an obligation to the Canadian people to oppose constructively and in a way that bears at least some relation to the realities of the complex world in which we live. Perhaps nothing better indicates the political and intellectual bankruptcy of the official opposition than the empty and mindless criticism of government economic policies contained in the motion put before the House today by the Leader of the Official Opposition.

Not only are his criticisms unsupported by the facts; they are flatly denied by the facts. Once again the Leader of the Opposition has failed to put forward comprehensive alternatives of his own by which the Canadian people could judge the policies that would be adopted by a Conservative government. It is quite remarkable, Mr. Speaker, what a close resemblance the Leader of the Opposition bears to a mythical Canadian political figure, conjured up recently by one of the country's eminent financial writers, whom he called Bob Er

April 24, 1972
Alleged. Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
Umm. It seems he decided on that name because every time he was asked what he would do differently than the government in power which he so strongly criticized, he replied, "Er umm."
In his motion the Conservative leader alleges that the House lacks confidence in the ability of the government to meet the needs and challenges of the seventies because of its failure to produce measures to create employment, to encourage investment in Canadian industry and because of widespread uncertainty caused by its economic programs. It is, I think, useful and instructive to take a hard look at those allegations which the Conservative leader advanced in his motion and elaborated in his speech even though he advanced no alternatives or suggestions.
Over the past two years the government has introduced a broad series of measures aimed at creating both directly and indirectly new jobs for Canadians. In a report issued late last year the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development in fact estimated that the Canadian government had injected substantially greater fiscal stimulus to promote the expansion of the economy than any major industrial nation. I do not think there is much room for doubt that these fiscal measures, together with the expansion of monetary policy, played a more important part in spurring a greater increase in Canada's real national output last year than those of any industrial country except Japan. Our increase was twice that of the United States and Germany.
I will not burden the House with a recital of all the measures which were brought forward in the form of tax cuts, increased federal spending and lending programs during this two-year period to promote increased production and employment in Canada. As an illustration of the magnitude of these measures, however, I would point out that the direct employment-related programs introduced in the House last October, such as the Local Initiatives Program, on-the-job training programs and the special loan and grant program to help finance capital projects by the provinces and municipalities this winter have involved federal expenditures alone of more than half a billion dollars.
The hon. member for York South arrogates to himself and to his party a monopoly of concern for the human aspects of unemployment. This hard-nosed, hard-bitten, high-priced union lawyer will find as much difficulty in maintaining that stance as he and his party are finding in convincing prairie farmers that the NDP has the interests of prairie farmers at heart.
To avoid being misunderstood or misconstrued by members of the opposition, let me hasten to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that I am well aware, and the government is well aware, that there are still too many Canadians without jobs who want to work. Certainly we on our side are not trying to hide the fact. Developing the means to create jobs for all Canadians who want to work continues to be the first priority of this government.

At the outset of my remarks I referred to the need in this country to face up to the realities of the

world in which we live. One of the hard realities confronting us, one which is no less real because the opposition chooses to ignore it, is that we in Canada are confronted by a unique and far reaching problem because our labour force is growing very much faster than that of any other industrial nation.
Over the past several years we have on the whole made tremendous strides in dealing with this problem. During the 1960's, the rate at which now jobs were created in Canada grew nine times faster than that in West Germany, nearly six times faster than that in Britain and four times faster than that in France. During the same period, the relative increase in employment in Canada was also 50 per cent greater than that in either the United States or Japan. During the first two years of the 1970's, employment increased three times more rapidly in Canada than it did south of the border.
The steady expansion of our economy, together with the direct job-creating measures adopted by the government, have helped to accelerate the growth of employment over the past several months. In March, the last month for which figures are available, there were 88,000 more Canadians with jobs than in February, an increase for that month which was exceeded only in the boom year of 1967. Total employment in March was up by 330,000, or 4.3 per cent, over the level a year ago which, as the Financial Times pointed out recently, represents a greater increase over the 12-month period than that which took place in any year in the booming 1960s. Nor is this just a one-month fluke. As the Financial Times also noted, the growth in employment over the period since last September has been at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of almost 6 per cent, which is extraordinarily high.
To claim, as the Leader of the Official Opposition has in his motion, that the government has failed to produce measures to create employment is completely contrary to the facts. The most charitable view it is possible to take is that at the very least the Conservative leader's allegation represents an exercise in self-deception. Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, it is a case of the wish being father to the thought. And what of the claim by the Leader of the Opposition that the government has failed to encourage investment in Canadian industry? Much the same may be said of this second allegation as of the first.
The fact is that the greatest source of encouragement to Canadian industry to step up its capital investment is a rapidly growing economy, which leads in turn to a rapid expansion of demand for its goods and services. As I have already pointed out, just such an expansion of the economy has been in progress now for a period of many months as a result of the fiscal and monetary stimulus injected by the federal government.
It is, of course, true that in the early stages of accelerated economic growth companies tend to make use of the existing, unused capacity of their plants and equipment to fill expanding demand for their goods and services, rather than to invest in new facilities. As the output of these facilities begins to get stretched to the limit, however, industry begins to step up its capital investment in order to increase its productive capacity.
Quite apart from the impetus to capital investment resulting from the healthy growth of the economy, there
April 24, 1972

have been a number of particular measures introduced over an extended period that were aimed directly at bolstering Canadian industry by strengthening its competitive position and facilitating expansion of capital investment. Just by way of example I might remind the House that in December, 1970, the government took steps to permit Canadian manufacturers and processors to write off depreciation on new capital investment at the rate of 115 per cent of actual cost. In the budget last June, the 3 per cent corporate surtax was abolished, along with that on personal incomes. In October, the total income tax payable by corporations was reduced by a further 7 per cent during the period from July 1, 1971, to the end of this year. Together with the abolition of the surtax, this represented a very substantial reduction in corporate taxes of 10 per cent.
During 1971, total capital investment in Canada increased by 11 per cent, which is well above the longterm average, although for the reasons I have already mentioned, by increase in business capital investment was more moderate. It is quite true that the initial survey of capital spending investment intentions for 1972 indicates a significant slowing down in the rate at which total capital investment will increase this year. But because this survey was taken around the turn of the year when there was still a high degree of uncertainty as a result of the international monetary crisis, there is every reason to believe that actual investment spending in 1972 will be considerably higher than forecast. Certainly conditions are ripe for an upward surge in capital investment by business to get under way in Canada to match that already anticipated in the United States.
Let me deal now with the third allegation by the leader of the opposition, namely, that the government has caused widespread uncertainty regarding its economic programs, which supposedly has also contributed to a lack of confidence in the ability of the government to meet the needs and challenges of the 1970s. With this allegation, the Conservative leader has outdone himself.
There is an old saying, Mr. Speaker, which I think has some application in this situation. It is that you cannot scramble an egg without breaking it. By the same token, you cannot change policies without creating some uncertainty. We live in a world of very rapid and far reaching changes. If we are to be able to meet the needs and challenges of the seventies we must respond to those changes which are occurring all about us, and nowhere more so than in the economic field. There are many conservatively minded people in this and other countries who refuse to recognize the need for change, who cling to the status quo and the conventional wisdom of the past.
There is plenty of room for argument among reasonable men about how we should respond to change, but in my view there is none whatever about the need to respond. During the period when new policies and programs are in the process of being formulated and debated, it is inevitable that there will be considerable controversy and uncertainty. I say that controversy and uncertainty are often inevitable, but perhaps on second thought I am mistaken. Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition will let us know if he has found a way of reshaping government policies and programs to meet the needs of today and
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
tomorrow without creating a measure of uncertainty in the process. Perhaps while he is at it he will also tell us how to scramble an egg without breaking it. And after that perhaps he will tell this House and the Canadian people just what policies and programs his party proposes to meet the challenges of the seventies.
I suppose that when the Conservative leader refers to widespread uncertainty regarding the government's economic programs, he is echoing the misgivings voiced within the business community over some of the measures introduced or being considered by the government to respond to the changing economic circumstances which confront us as a nation. In this connection I was much interested in a statement placed as an advertisement in the New York Times a few days ago by a very large United States corporation, Mobil Oil Company, under the heading, "Business is bound to change". I would like to read some excerpts from that statement because I think it is highly relevant. It provides more than sufficient answers to the Leader of the Opposition, and indeed to those in the business community itself who have criticized us for causing uncertainty. The statement begins:
Change upsets people. Always has. Disrupts routine and habit patterns. Demands constant adaptation.
But change is inevitable. And essential. Inability to change can be fatal.
Unfortunately, most of man's institutions are highly resistant to change.
This, as much as anything else, underlies the explosive reaction of many people in our country in the past few years. They took a fresh and uncluttered look at the world around them, and found many institutions archaic. Higher education. Government. Religion, business.
These institutions have begun to respond to the need for change, even if not always with breathtaking speed.
Among these institutions, business is by the nature of things compelled to change more rapidly-and perhaps more realistically-if it is to survive. Companies that cannot foresee change and adapt to it quickly enough die. There is seldom anybody to subsidize business inefficiency for any length of time.
One reason business-especially big business-can respond to change quickly is that basically it is in the business of change. Business depends heavily on forward planning, and planning is the orderly management of change.
Another reason-
If I could, I would heavily underline this passage, Mr. Speaker.
-is that business itself produces more change, probably, than any other institution. Through its research and development programs. Through new technology it develops and applies. Through new plants it builds. Through its need to be a good employer. Because its own long-term self-interest dictates a better life for people everywhere. Because it must face facts and think rationally about what may appear to be unthinkable.
If there is a measure of uncertainty, it is precisely because this government has moved to respond to change for the very purpose of meeting the needs and challenges of the 1970s. The leader of the Conservative party may rejoice in the belief that neither he nor his party has to face facts or to think rationally about what may be unthinkable, but I am convinced the Canadian people have enough plain, ordinary common sense to know that they cannot indulge in the same luxury if they hope to

speechtext:
That is completely incorrect. With regard to the island of Cape Breton-these are not my estimates but those of action groups and welfare officials in Sydney and other areas-there is an unemployment rate of anywhere from 20 to 25 per cent, despite LIP and the Opportunities for Youth program. I suggest to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration that these are temporary measures, providing employment for a short period of time. This is all well and good and we are very glad that those taking part thought of something. The government was bankrupt of ideas and could not think of anything to provide employment so it said, "Okay, you fellows; provide something and we will give you the money." I am glad the government has done this, but what permanency is there in these programs so far as employment is concerned? I suggest these jobs last only a few weeks or a few months.
Then we had the holus-bolus idea of throwing grants out in various areas to people who are wasting the money. I have discussed this matter with members of the government. There must be some way of checking more carefully on the use of this money. Other people have had extremely good ideas which have been rejected because they are not unique. I will not go into that question now because we will have more time later on to do so.
Let me say this to those hon. gentlemen who say we have made no suggestions. They have allowed freight rates in the Atlantic provinces to increase time and time again under this administration. They have done nothing about this. As a result, businessmen as well as labour in the area are concerned. One businessman told me the other day that he sent to Guelpn for a small piece of equipment which cost $3.90, and it cost $4.20 to ship it to him.
No matter how often members of the government side stand in this chamber and say there are many thousands more working now than a month ago, six months ago or ten years ago, this does nothing for the 800,000 who are not working. I am looking at some Ontario members who perhaps do not face this situation, but in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia and throughout the Atlantic provinces we come in contact with people who are well trained and willing to take any type of job but cannot find employment.
April 24, 1972

There was a man in my office when I was at home over the weekend who is a well trained cement finisher. I worked with him in the coal mines some years ago. He has a wife in the hospital, and a very sick child. He has tried everywhere to obtain employment. I have contacted Manpower on his behalf, but he cannot get employment. I finally said that we would have to get welfare for him, and he blew his top. He said he was not going on welfare; he wanted to work. He then said he was sorry for blowing up at me and realized that I was trying to do something for him. He said he had not been on welfare ever during his lifetime and did not want to go on welfare now. This is the heartbreaking type of case involving people who cannot find employment that we become aware of every day. There are thousands of cases like this. We can mention all the figures we want in this House, but that will not help the situation.
The government and this man who is part-time Prime Minister have created a climate of uncertainty in the public service, uncertainty in the ranks of organized and unorganized labour, uncertainty in the business world and uncertainty in the armed forces. These people do not know where they will be tomorrow, and even senior officers in the service are speaking out about the situation. The government has created a climate of uncertainty in the fishing industry and in almost every area one could mention.
This government and our part-time Prime Minister have created a climate of uncertainty all across the land. What do they intend to do about unemployment? When are they going to put people back to work? Let me quote from a memorandum presented to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the government of Canada on March 6, 1972. These are the remarks of a Cape Bretoner. I am not referring to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. MacEachen) but to Donald MacDonald, president of the Canadian Labour Congress. He states in this brief:
When we appeared before you a year ago, we said that never before had we felt such a profound sense of concern about the affairs of our nation.
He went on to say:
High unemployment, which has long afflicted Canada, continues to be the number one national problem. Not only was there no let-up, no relief from this scourge in 1971, but, on the contrary, the unemployment rate rose to its highest level in ten years.
He went on to say that when he appeared before the Prime Minister a year earlier he expressed considerable pessimism, which was called unjustified, about the prospect of any significant dent being made in unemployment for the year ahead. He said:
But we are not in a mood to say that "we told you so". We are not in a mood to score debating points over an issue involving the plight of hundreds of thousands of Canadian workers and their families. Furthermore, as pessimistic as we were on that occasion, we could be properly chastised today for not having foreseen more clearly the degree to which unemployment would accelerate in 1971. The sorry fact is that the official unemployment data indicate only too clearly that 1971 was a year of disaster.
This was a year of disaster under a part-time Prime Minister who in the last few months has shown his great interest in the House and in the monarchy! Even today he sat in the House while the Leader of the Opposition made a speech. We have seen this under the Pearson govern-
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment ment, the St. Laurent government, the Diefenbaker government and the Mackenzie King government, but we have not seen it often under this Prime Minister: he will not even take the time to listen to the Leader of the Opposition or the leader of the NDP. He might get some good ideas, but he will not listen. The Prime Minister can say many things in the comfort of his Cadillac, but not here.
We heard the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce say that the Leader of the Opposition was spreading doom and gloom. He is a great comedian but he did not get any laughs. He did receive a little bit of applause from two nuts on the government side who had nothing else to do, but he received no applause from his other colleagues. He accused the Leader of the Opposition of spreading doom and gloom. No one has to spread doom and gloom today; it is an actual fact. The people of Canada are fed up with the arrogance and complacency of someone who does not realize, does not know and has never experienced unemployment. He has never had the feeling of having to meet the rent or the grocery bill with his pockets empty.
Liberal members say this government did not create unemployment. This government certainly did create unemployment, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). The Prime Minister said in December, 1969, that we should watch the government because it was going to defeat inflation no matter what happened. He said that unemployment could go up to 6 per cent or even higher and he would not worry about it. Those were his words. I can understand his lack of concern. This is a man who does not worry about unemployment.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) are willing to give consideration to many things but they are always overruled. They are not among the top echelon of this government. They are not part of the troika or the three or four who run this country. They do not have the opportunity to do something about unemployment.
He did not suggest to the Lapalme workers that they should eat cake. Whether the Lapalme workers were right or wrong, do you in reality and good sense, Mr. Speaker, think the Prime Minister should push a button in his air conditioned, bullet-proof car and yell out the window at people who are demonstrating? This is the man who talked about participatory democracy. He did not tell them to eat cake, but something far worse. This is the attitude of our so-called Prime Minister. What was said to one hon. member when he asked the Prime Minister a question about unemployment? What the Prime Minister said, later turned out to be "fuddle-duddle". Those of us who were here know what he said.
On another occasion an hon. member from Newfoundland was speaking on behalf of his constituents who needed employment. But this great man sits over there, looks across at the Conservatives, the NDP and Social Credit members and says, "These peasants, what are they questioning me about? I know what is good for the people". We know how much time he spends in this House. For three years he roamed all around the world, and finally this year he sticks a lot closer to home. Is he looking after the unemployed, or is he planning an elec-

This is the kind of man we have for Prime Minister. What is he doing for the unemployed except putting up just two or three speakers who say there are so many thousands of people doing this and that. One can use statistics and computers, but this will not put bread on the tables of the unemployed. How long must we put up with this climate of uncertainty?
Now I will get closer to questions concerning my constituency. The Cape Breton Development Corporation took over, from the Department of Transport, the Point Edward industrial park two years ago. The union there cannot negotiate. The operation was taken over but was not legally transferred from the Department of Transport. Time and time again we attempted to have something done about this. On june 10 the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) wrote a letter to me saying:
I am sorry to have been slow to reply to your letter of March 18. I have been waiting for what I hoped would be Devco's finalization of arrangements about the Point Edward industrial park.
While these have not yet been completed, there is no question of the men concerned losing benefits that they had when they were employees of the Department of Transport. That was a commitment.
These men are losing benefits, so apparently it was not a firm commitment. There is a climate of uncertainty in the public service. I supported and voted for the official languages bill and I believe it is a wonderful thing but, like the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Blair), I have concerns and worries about it for the simple reason that an eligibility list that was set up in Cape Breton some months ago, and which should have been good to June 15, 1972, is to be changed. It was established on December 20, 1971, and dealt with the positions of five customs officers in North Sydney and Sydney. As of June they are going to do away with the eligibility list and thereby deprive the people who have written the exam of the opportunity of employment. They are to use a list under which bilingualism is a prerequisite. Like the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton I do not think we should move so fast on these matters. However, I voted for the languages bill and I still believe it is a good bill. I believe in B and B, but are we to destroy the bread and butter features of this whole situation?
We talk about unemployment. The Minister of Labour is on record as saying that it takes a lot of courage to create unemployment. This government created unemployment. It slowed down the economy. It cooled it off so badly that it is frozen and the government cannot get it moving. Then the Prime Minister said, "Like it or lump it. If you don't like what I do, throw me out". The arrogance is there. This man is destroying our country not only economically but morally and in every other way. The sooner he is out of office, the better-and the better it will be for the unemployed.
