subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I might be permitted to put into ordinary language the thrust of the motion we are discussing today, I would

suggest that the thought which comes out of it is: Where are we headed? I believe this is the question which today is uppermost in the minds of the Canadian population. What is the direction, what is the hope in the future for the individual? What is the hope in the future for business? Really this is what we are talking about in this House today.
As I have said, the question which today seems uppermost in the minds of many people is that we in Canada seem to have lost a sense of direction. No one seems to know where we are headed. Business does not know. We have the example of the tremendous decrease in capital outlay in the first quarter of this year, and we have the statement made a few moments ago by the Minister of State (Mr. Mahoney) that all is well and that we should hang on a little longer because we will see a tremendous upsurge in the economy. This reminds me of some of the famous last words of the former minister of finance who had unemployment licked. He said we should just wait until the next report came out and then it would be seen that we had turned the corner. He was completely off the track because we had more unemployment and more inflation.
Agriculture does not know where it is headed. We have had all types of proposals for the agricultural industry. We have had announcements about farm enlargement. We have had task forces recommending that inefficient small farmers be moved off the farms, retrained and placed in other occupations. Then we have had the latest one, the family farm enlargement program which the minister announced several months ago. This created a lot of interest and enthusiasm among the younger farmers in this country who were preparing to enlarge their holdings. This is the program under which the older farmer could remain in the house on the farm and would not be uprooted while the young fellow took over. The minister knows all about it but the head office of the Farm Credit Corporation does not know anything about it. They do not know when it is to come into effect. The minister, however, grabbed all the publicity he possibly could from a very nebulous type of program which has not yet been implemented. There is always hope that it may come about.
Labour leaders, business leaders, teachers, brokers, firemen, bootmakers and even the proverbial candlestick-maker-no one knows what way to turn. But what does emerge from all of this is that we have one absolutely concrete thrust: this government, aided by its computers, academics and associated eggheads and its power-hungry adherents, seems to feel it has a God-given right that it is better qualified to spend the citizen's money and to order his life than he himself. That is the only genuine thrust.
Let us take an example. We have heard talk in this chamber, over lo these many years, about the CDC, the Canada Development Corporation. Now, at long last, this worthy organization through its chairman has offered to take Polymer Corporation and the Northern Navigation Company off the hands of the Canadian public. It has offered to take over these well-run, efficient Crown corporations. I say to the CDC that if it wants a challenge, it should be interested in taking over the CBC or the CNR. I
April 24, 1972

question the value of this organization except to build up more government bureaucracy.
It is my humble opinion that some reasonable income tax incentives directed toward investment in Canadian industry and development would be far more practical and effective. Further, there would be no necessity for more empire building. Surely somebody, some organization could come up with a list of projects including resource development, manufacturing and services- investment in which one could enjoy tax incentives. If individuals were helped in this way, I believe it would do more in one year to get ownership of our resources into Canadian hands than the CDC will accomplish in its lifetime. But instead of giving reasonable incentives we establish another bureaucracy. The thrust is still there, Mr. Speaker. Under government supervision we are to invest in the Canada Development Corporation. And if you do invest, be prepared to pay capital gains tax. Again we have Big Brother looking over our shoulder and telling us what it is best to do.
I do not think there is need for me to dwell on the so-called tax reform measures that we had before us in the House last year except to ask, where are the 100 or so amendments promised by the former minister of finance as he slowly pulled away and sank into the sunset, buried forever in the Department of National Defence, the place where we have three, or is it five non-commissioned officers for every private? Is this the stuff of which confidence is built?
What about the great improvements to the Post Office promised by that fearless administrator from Duvernay? He accomplished one thing, and that was higher taxes. Here I refer to postage as a tax. The tax is away up and services are away down. Now once more we have the possibility of six-day service. There is an interesting little piece in today's Ottawa Journal about that matter:
Around the world with Liberal efficiency! To save money, the five-day mail week. To save more money, back to the six-day system.
What does the government take us for? Perhaps Mr. Cote thought that confession would make him seem a refreshingly different kind of politician, or would at least be good for his soul.
Well, maybe. But it is an open admission that the Post Office has not known what it was doing, that the vaunted business efficiency and reforms which Eric Kierans was supposed to have introduced were pure myth-
What Canadians do feel strongly about is being gulled by cabinet ministers who have been trying to sell higher mail rates and poorer service at the same time.
That is the whole thrust of this debate. Where are we going? What are we getting for our money? A few years ago the government presided over the death of an industry in southwestern Ontario. It paid $1 million to farmers in southwestern Ontario not to grow sugar beet. Of course, that was during an election period. All that was needed to save the industry at that time was a little government direction, a statement to the effect that we should have a national sugar policy, that we as Canadians must produce a percentage of our own needs. Instead, the industry was allowed to die. The result has been depression among the farmers in that area.
That decision took 20,000 or 30,000 acres of land out of production. Yet this afternoon the Minister of Agriculture
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
(Mr. Olson) had the temerity to say-I think I quote him fairly accurately-that the situation is better now than when the industry was closed. He was replying to a question by my colleague from Kent-Essex (Mr. Danforth) who was referring to an article in the Globe and Mail of April 22 which stated that Austin Sugar Refineries Ltd. of Montreal plans to build a refinery in Cornwall. I think it is great that Cornwall should have a refinery. That company will receive a $665,000 incentive grant which will produce 100 to 110 jobs. But all this will be, in effect, is a bagging operation. Cane sugar is to be imported, refined a little and bagged at Cornwall.
A little money invested in re-establishing a whole industry in southwestern Ontario could provide 200 or 300 jobs, plus added income from diversification by hundreds of farmers in the area. We are not a designated area and that may have some bearing on the situation. But we are not receiving direction from government on how to establish a genuine, made-in-Canada sugar policy. That is what is wrong and that is what we are missing.
When the sugar industry in southern Ontario was phased out, the farmers had to diversify. But they did not receive any direction from this government. In Essex, Kent, Middlesex, Lambton-all over the southern part of Ontario farmers tell me that it is extremely difficult, if not impossible, to get a contract today to grow tomatoes. They are anxious to get into the business. The Department of Agriculture must know that, and if the minister were on his toes he would pass the information along to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand). It does not seem to me that he has bothered to do this. If he had, why would this government give a grant of over half a million dollars to Catelli Foods, which I understand is a subsidiary of General Foods in the United States, to establish a plant in the St. Lawrence area? The sole purpose of this plant is to process tomato paste imported from Portugal, Spain, Italy, Yugoslavia or wherever it can be bought cheaply. This goes on whilst Canadian farmers cannot obtain contracts to grow tomatoes because there are not enough contracts to go round.
No wonder people are asking where we are going. Mr. Speaker, I say it is time that we in Canada established our priorities and a common sense of purpose, which we have not been doing in the past. Leacock's description of the horseman who mounted and then rode off in all directions is a classic example of this government. On January 1, 1972, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), with great fanfare announced that there would be no more cigarette advertising on radio and television- down with tar and nicotine! Virtually on the same day that $200,000 was spent on an anti-smoking campaign, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion made the following announcement:
Dominion Cigarette Tube Company Limited of Montreal will receive an incentive of approximately $48,000 for a new plant to produce cigarette paper tubes which will employ an estimated 67 persons. The development incentive is based on a rate of 5 per cent of the approved capital costs, estimated at $300,000, plus $500 for each new job created.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the no-confidence motion tabled by the hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) reads and I quote:
That because the Government has failed to produce measures to create employment, has failed to encourage investment in Canadian industry, and has caused widespread uncertainty as to its economic programmes-
My colleagues, the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Perrault) recalled this afternoon certain measures which the government had taken to promote employment. The Minister of State (Mr. Mahoney) also mentioned tonight the incentives and other measures to which the government had resorted.
I would like to speak at this point about our exports which are of great importance for the maintenance and creation of jobs in Canada.
This is why the government, through the federal Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, offers our national industry a very large choice of tools in order either to help Canadian exporters break into new foreign markets, or consolidate and develop their position on already existing ones.
The department has also initiated commercial negotiations, particularly to improve the conditions of access of Canadian products to foreign markets. Our trade commissioners have granted 80 stations in 57 countries a financial assistance similar to that recently accorded to facilitate the establishment of submissions concerned with investment projects abroad, to prospect new markets and adjust marketing.
For some years past, commercial and departmental delegations have increasingly served as instruments for commercial promotion. They play a very important role in the endeavours of Canada to diversify her trade and increase her exports to markets other than the United States.
This does not mean, Mr. Speaker, to transfer our exports from the American market to other markets, but rather to keep and strengthen our position in relation to the United States, and do better elsewhere.
Here are a few economic and ministerial missions which have done their task in 1971 and early 1972. From April 14 to 22, 1971, a Canadian trade and industrial mission visited the Federal Republic of Germany in order to establish stronger commercial bounds between that country and Canada. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) headed this mission which included 28 Canadian businessmen and industrialists, as well as representatives of the federal and provincial governments. The delegates visited major trade and industrial centres in Germany, including Bonn, Dusseldorf, Cologne, Frankfurt, Hanover and Wolfsburg.

Canada established diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China on October 13, 1970. In order to promote Sino-Canadian relations in all areas, an economic and trade mission led by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) visited China from June 28 to July 4, 1971. This mission was composed of representatives of various federal departments, namely Industry, Trade and Commerce, Agriculture, National Revenue, Energy, Mines and Ressources, and External Affairs. There were also representatives of various trade and industrial organizations in Canada, of groups connected with agriculture, forestry, pulp and paper, mining, manufacture, chemicals, industry, trade, banking, engineering, exports and imports. Those people had friendly and constructive talks with Prime Minister Chou En-Lai, with the ministers of external trade, of agriculture, of forestry, and of light industry, as well as with the deputy ministers responsible for the metallurgic industry, the fuel industry, and the chemical industry.
From November 17 to 24, 1972, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce was in Rome, and when he left the Italian capital, he went to Algeria, where he led a trade mission composed of 17 Canadian businessmen and a group of public servants and Crown corporation officers.
From December 6 to 18, 1971, a group of 12 Canadian agriculture experts led by Mr. R. P. Poirier, Assistant Deputy Minister of the Department of Agriculture, took part in an agriculture and trade mission to the U.S.S.R. The purpose of this mission was to explore opportunities for information and technology exchanges, with a view to reaching licensing agreements, and eventually to increasing trade between our two countries in the agricultural and commercial fields.
In December 1971, a trade and economic mission headed by the Minister of Industry and Commerce went to Morocco in search of ways and means of developing closer trade and economic ties with that North African country.
With a view to increasing our efforts to sell manufactured good on the Japanese market, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce headed a trade mission which visited Japan from January 21 to 29, 1972; 31 business and industrial representatives accompanied him. This was the largest Canadian delegation of its type ever to go to that country. During the same period, economic and ministerial missions came to Canada from various countries including the USSR and Japan.
Mr. Speaker, other means, including participation in industrial exhibitions and fairs and others, both national and international, were used to stimulate our sales promotion. This promotion is being pursued in close co-operation with the private sector of industry, the federal government and, in some cases, with provincial authorities.
There has been Canadian participation to a certain number of fairs and exhibitions. During the first week of March 1971, 15 Canadian corporations took part in the New England Boat Show in Boston. At the 52th National Conference and Educational Exhibition of Restaurants, Hotels and Motels held in Chicago from May 22 to May 26 1971, 26 Canadian corporations exhibited goods such as
April 24, 1972

equipment, kitchen furniture and food products for the restaurant, hotel and motel industry. For the second year, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce was sponsoring Canadian participation to that event. Canadian editors, English-speaking as well as French-speaking, for the first time shared a stand at the 61st International Book Exhibition held in Dallas (Texas) from June 20 to June 24 1971.
At the beginning of December 1971, ten Canadian textile manufacturers who had exhibited at the Interstoff Show held in Frankfurt (Germany) obtained orders for some $6 million. Canadian sales of $6 million almost doubled compared with those of the previous show.
For the first time, Canadian products will be shown at an exclusively Canadian commercial exhibition in Peking from August 21 to September 2, 1972. The exhibition, which will occupy an area of 140,000 square feet, will comprise a wide range of equipment and industrial products. It will be the largest Canadian exhibition ever organized-over 200 Canadian companies will show their products; the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce will be responsible for this project and its organization. The participation of Canadian companies in such fairs and exhibitions has undoubtedly resulted in millions of dollars of orders placed at the exhibitions and for considerably larger amounts as a result of re-orders.
On August 15, 1971, the United States imposed a 10 per cent surcharge on imports, which has been discontinued as from December 20, 1971. As early as September 7, 1971, the Canadian government introduced an Employment Support Bill to offset the United States surcharge. On February 18, 1972, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce announced that on December 31, 1971, a total of $3,311,703 had been awarded as grants to 178 firms by the Employment Support Board to protect 7,727 jobs.
Mr. Speaker, we must continue to look for new incentives, new ways and new methods of increasing our exports which, in 1971, represented $17,847 billion compared with $16,910 billion in 1970.
In closing, I would like to point out that the Leader of the Opposition stated this afternoon that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) should present a budget. But I must tell him that he is a member of the party that was in power from 1958 to 1962 under the direction of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). Now, during that period, the Canadian government did not present any budget for a period of 16 months, that is from December 20, 1960 to April 10, 1962.

We have been presenting motions during budget debates, Throne Speech debates and on various other occasions throughout the past three years, all to do with the same theme, namely, this administration's total inability to deal with the problems of infla-
Alleged. Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
tion and employment and some of the problems of taxation.
Oh, yes, they have brought in tax changes. The same author who put on paper what the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney) said tonight must have written what went into the white paper on taxation back in 1970. In both cases there was the same prose by the flacks. There was hardly any change. Strangely enough, the hon. member's words seemed to be inspired by the sort of attitude that is often demonstrated by hon. members opposite, that is, that theirs is the inspiration of more than mortal men, that it is almost divinely inspired.
In their opinion, since they have been elected to this House, even though sometimes the people were deceived in electing them, they may assume the mantle of omniscience. Well, I listened to the former parliamentary secretary-I am sorry; he was the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance but now he is the Minister of State attached to the Minister of Finance: perhaps we should call him the minister from Calgary South and leave it at that.

The hon. member was not even here in those years. He was not here from 1958 to 1962, so he cannot tell. In any event, it is not part of the program. Many members opposite, including the Minister of State, have had their nominations. They are expecting an election. However, we will not get the government's program. We have not heard of it. We have not heard of the program from members to my left. The program of this party will be disclosed. An election campaign is the time for disclosure of programs and the choice to be made is for the people. But what does he think when the Leader of the Opposition talks about tax cuts on building materials? What about tax measures with regard to corporations? What about credits for capital gains paid on death as against succession duties? They are specific fiscal measures.
What does the Minister of State want? If he wants more, there are the recommendations of the joint committee of the Canadian Bar and Canadian Chartered Accountants with regard to the tax measures planned which the Minister of State spent so much time lauding this afternoon. All he did was sit stolidly for three or four months last fall while members of the opposition and some members on the government side tried to get improvements made to

The then Minister of Finance did not dare face this House to put through his bill; he had to get someone else to do it. We know he went to the Senate. It would be hard to say he bribed the Senate, but I will say that he certainly conned the majority of the members of the Senate with promises of early tax changes before they became completely and utterly bound up in the web of the economy and our taxation system. What happened? We have not heard one iota about those tax changes.
We asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) to give us a budget. He must give a financial accounting of what has happened since last June. He could tell us that he intends to present a budget in the early part of May and what measures the government is going to take. Is there going to be a budget, or is this House going to be dismissed for an election and the Canadian electorate told to lump it, so that the government will not have to disclose the financial state of the nation until perhaps September? Is that what is going to happen?
Is the Minister of Finance afraid to disclose that the budgetary deficit may be between $1 billion and $1,200 million? Is the government afraid to disclose its foreign ownership policy? Is this going to be leaked, or will it come out in a way in which it cannot be debated? The hon. member says it will be debated during an election campaign. That is not a debate that is subject to the searching scrutiny of this House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO INTRODUCE MEASURES TO ENCOURAGE INVESTMENT AND CREATE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
How many meetings does the hon. member think he is going to address in his constituency in order to explain foreign ownership? How many people does he think he can get together in the spring of the year? There is no way the government can explain that policy to the people. It is only as a result of continuous debate in this House that the weaknesses in any program can be exposed to the public.
We will see how bankrupt of ideas this government is with regard to foreign ownership. What is the government prepared to do? Are they going to be a party of repression? Is this to be a program of repressive regulations, thou shalt nots, or are we to go out and ask people to have faith in Canada and encourage them to invest in their industry? That is something that can be done. That is part of our program in so far as incentives may be offered.
The government talks about uncertainty. The greatest uncertainty has been in the field of business ownership in this country. In 1968 this government brought forward the most savage Estate Tax Act one could contemplate. It is absolutely punitive in its levies. It was disguised under public legislation but it is a system of legalized plunder and piracy by people motivated by desire for the have-nots to take from the haves. This is an antiquated tool that has no place in the Canadian economy. The estate tax was eliminated in 1971 by Bill C-259. However, some of the provinces rushed in to increase or impose succession duties. Also, the Canadian public is still faced with a capital gains tax. All this creates uncertainty. The regulations for capital gains were not published until the other day. The same thing applies to corporations. There was a

great rush to have the act effective January 1. For months Canadians did not know the bulk of the tax regulations. They are not even out yet in respect of partnerships.
This is supposed to be an administration that talks of certainty. Certainty? What a mockery they have made of the word. It is uncertainty with regard to foreign ownership and it is uncertainty with regard to the activities of the Canada Development Corporation, another supposed jewel in the crown of this administration. All they have done is name a president and a few directors. Nothing has happened with regard to the Canada Development Corporation. They have decided to do something only for a few milk cows in the form of Crown corporations, those that are paying returns. If a Crown corporation is not paying any dividends and is not in a profit position, it will not be taken over by the Canada Development Corporation. The transparency of that move should be apparent to the blindest member of this House.
I am pleased to see that in many ways the province of Quebec, in the budget delivered the other night, saw that going after succession duties, as has been done by so many provincial administrations, was self-defeating and that they are moving ultimately to eliminate them. I am glad the province of Ontario is trying to get out of that field. I hope some of the other provinces follow the example which was set by my own province in this respect. Alberta did not even get into succession duties, because succession duties and the heavy level of death duties has been one of the greatest contributors to foreign ownership of Canadian industry. This has been the cause of great uncertainty over the years.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) has been charing about the country disposing of grants here, there and everywhere, unworried whether the operation in connection with which the largesse is being dispensed would be closed in a couple of years or that maybe a plant 50 miles away would be closed as a result. It is all a matter of the amount of money involved. The big question is: where has the bulk of money been spent, and what has been the result? This is what we want to know. After all, it is money from British Columbia too. I can see that the hon. member for Vancouver South, the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Laing), knows how much money-

It is all part of an industrial pattern. The province of British Columbia has not benefited from it; the province of Alberta has not benefited. We have seen more industries close. The minister from Calgary South frowns. Let him ask the minister of economic development of the province of Alberta, or he
April 24, 1972

could ask the deputy minister or the ex-deputy minister. They could tell him how many industries have closed in Alberta because they could not compete or get enough capital for necessary development because it was being given to other regions of the country. This is part of the price one has to pay.
Last year when we were examining the estimates of the Economic Council of Canada I moved a motion that the Economic Council, which has plenty of authority to do this work, should conduct an objective assessment of the policies and programs of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. Authority to do this is specifically mentioned in the act setting up the council. But no: government members were too frightened of it and the motion was thrown out. But the motion was right. This is the sort of thing the Economic Council was designed to do.
The present administration is creating more uncertainty by putting pressure on people in the Economic Council to change its attitude so that it might be more amenable to government wishes. We remember the criticism the deputy minister of finance directed toward the Economic Council. He does not feel he has an amenable tool under his control. It is all very well to discourage the chairman from continuing, and to have the vice-chairman transferred to another position. If this administration were to continue, we would see what would happen to the Economic Council. The council was not telling the government the things it wanted to hear; this is why changes were proposed and why changes are being made in the council.
The limit of my time is now approaching, Mr. Speaker, and I should like to make two further comments. With regard to the relationship between the government of Canada and the provincial administrations I would say this: the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) allegedly made his national reputation on television because of the way he dealt with the late premier of the province of Quebec. He was to be the man who would save national unity.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) said this was to be the great issue. Ask the Secretary of State what he thinks now about the relationship between the Prime Minister of Canada and the Premier of British Columbia, after the statement made by the Prime Minister. What does he think about the relationship between the Premier of Alberta and the Prime Minister? Has he read the speeches of the Premier of Alberta in recent days? What about Ontario? What about Quebec? We see there is a change in pattern. Is there a relationship on all hands which tends to unify Canada? Oh, no; the Prime Minister is setting about the ears of the premiers of the provinces. Does he get more co-operation from them now than he did in 1968 when he took office? If he believes so, he is the only one who is under that illusion. He is under an illusion and to that extent there is greater uncertainty.
The amendment to our motion moved by the New Democratic Party calls for a tax system which would ensure a fairer distribution of wealth. Well, income tax as it now exists is a means of redistributing wealth. There is nothing specific in the amendment. We would certainly like to see greater changes in the Income Tax Act, including much greater incentives. There would be a more equal
Alleged Failure to Alleviate Unemployment
distribution of income to all Canadians as a result of such changes. To this extent we are prepared to accept their amendment. Anyway, it is another indictment of this administration and it is very difficult to restrain oneself from making such indictments. This government have worn out their time and they should go.

speechtext:
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals have worn out their time and they should go, but the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has done very much the same thing to me.
I listened with great interest, as I always do, to the speech of the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Mahoney). While I was listening, I was trying to make up my mind which of two things was happening. Had they elevated the hon. member for Calgary South to such an exalted position that he could speak on behalf of the government in this important debate, or was the government so contemptuous of the arguments which the opposition was putting forward, and so unfeeling about unemployment, that they did not feel called upon to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) or the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to speak in this instance?
When we examine the argument which the Minister of State put up, it becomes obvious why the government sent a boy to do the job. The arguments fall apart. What the government is saying, in effect, is this: We have created more jobs than have been created in other countries; our labour force is larger. It is therefore not our fault there is so much unemployment; it is the fault of the people who decided to snuggle up to each other in this country about 20 years ago.
In fact, the government has known for 20 years that this situation would arise. That is not their fault; they simply ignored the problem, hoping that it would go away. But it did not go away and so we are faced with this shameful situation. The Liberal government stands indicted for its lack of foresight and its inability to solve the problems that face this nation.
I was particularly upset when the hon. member for Calgary South spoke with such feeling about tax reform in Canada. There has been no tax reform in this country and he, better than most, should know that. The government has backtracked on every single measure it has brought in; it has not stuck with anything. One of the reasons we have so much unemployment in this country is the failure of the taxation system to move us away from resource development to manufacturing industry.
The Liberal party, as it relates its activities to the businessmen of this country, might draw some inspiration from Shakespeare. It seems as though they are deserting the Liberal party and have found a new favourite in the Conservatives. I understand the Conservative party are loaded with money and are as proud as punch of it. They have all kinds of money because the traditional friends of the Liberals have deserted them. This reminds me of the speech of Cardinal Wolsey, who turns and with great sadness says:
O Cromwell, Cromwell!
Had I but served my God with half the zeal

I served my king, he would not in mine age
Have left me naked to mine enemies.
Had the Liberal party paid as much attention to the ordinary things in this country as it has to backtracking and meeting the objections of the businessmen, then I do not think they would face the rather desperate situation they will face in the coming election. Having given everything away, they have the nerve to say that they brought in tax reform in Canada. Admittedly, there were some changes made to exemption levels. Indeed, no measure can be totally bad. But tax reform it was not.
Despite the fact that there has been no capital gains tax for years, when the Liberal party finally decided to institute such a tax it was only half a tax. The oil industry still retains its privileges. The government of Alberta, the province from which the hon. member for Calgary South comes, is having difficulty with the oil industry at the moment. They are shafting Alberta as they have been shafting others. I read in the newspapers that industry is moving into Alberta but that the oil industry financed all its exploration work by tax concessions received from the United States government.
This oil industry has now found a new love. It is in the north, with the Eskimos and the bears, polluting the environment. It is in an area that is nice and clean and has hitherto been untouched. It is now getting money from the people of Canada to move into the north.
